sources.title: IDC: Worldwide smartphone market to decline 13.9% in 2026 as memory crisis constrains growth
sources.claims: Worldwide smartphone shipments forecast to fall 13.9% in 2026 to 1.09bn units, then -1.1% in 2027 and +5.5% in 2028; record ASP of $550 in 2026, up $100 year on year; North America -6.3% with 60% of Q1 2026 shipments above $800; China -13%; Android -21%; iOS to reach its highest-ever 22% share in 2026 with Apple shipments down only 5.2%; Huawei HarmonyOS 62m units in 2026; foldables +20% in 2026 with Apple entering in H2 2026; sub-$100 segment becomes unviable.
sources.claims_weakened: Any claim that the smartphone market is growing in units through 2026-2027; unit-volume-based growth stories for Apple. Shows the value pool is set by price, not volume.

sources.title: IDC: China smartphone market decline, Q2 2026 vendor shares
sources.claims: China smartphone shipments ~66m units in Q2 2026, -4.3% YoY, fifth consecutive quarterly decline; H1 2026 ~134m units, -4.2%; vendor shares Q2 2026: Huawei 22.6% (+19.4% YoY), Apple 18.1% (+24.4%), OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% (-21.7%), Honor 11.3%; top six ~96%; H2 2026 decline could widen to ~20%; recovery around 2028-2029.
sources.claims_weakened: The claim that Apple is losing China share to Huawei without interruption: Apple gained 4.2pp of China share YoY in Q2 2026 while Xiaomi, vivo and OPPO lost share.

sources.title: IDC: Worldwide smartphone top-5 shipments and share, Q1 2026
sources.claims: Q1 2026 global smartphone shipments 293.8m units, -2.9% YoY, ending ten quarters of growth; top-5 Q1 2026: Samsung 62.4m (21.2%), Apple 61.8m (21.0%), Xiaomi 33.8m (11.5%), OPPO 30.7m (10.5%), vivo 21.2m (7.2%); Apple iPhone 17 grew over 30% in China in Q1 2026; Samsung regained top position on Galaxy S26 Ultra; only Samsung and Apple grew among the top five; premiumisation to continue as memory prices stabilise in H2 2027.
sources.claims_weakened: Any claim that Apple holds a durable global unit-share lead over Samsung: Samsung led Q1 2026 21.2% versus Apple 21.0%, a statistical tie.

sources.title: Joint statement from Google and Apple
sources.claims: Apple and Google entered a multi-year collaboration (2026-01-12) under which the next generation of Apple Foundation Models will be based on Google's Gemini models and Google cloud technology; Apple Intelligence continues to run on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute. Confirms Apple licenses a frontier model rather than building one at the frontier.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens the claim that Apple's own foundation models are at the frontier; makes Gemini a critical third-party dependency.

sources.title: iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo Feature Apple's New C2 Modem
sources.claims: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and the foldable iPhone Duo unveiled 2026-09-09; prices $1,199 / $1,299 / $1,999; Duo pre-orders 2026-10-16, availability 2026-10-23. C2 custom modem in iPhone 18 Pro and Duo, mmWave in US (n258, n260, n261), 15% less energy than C1X, faster uploads; iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem. N1 Apple wireless chip (Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread).
sources.claims_weakened: Complicates the "Apple has replaced Qualcomm" narrative: the largest Pro Max SKU and some regions still appear to use Qualcomm modems.

sources.title: Private Cloud Compute: A new frontier for AI privacy in the cloud
sources.claims: Private Cloud Compute architecture: stateless computation on personal data, no privileged runtime access even for Apple staff, custom Apple silicon servers, verifiable transparency via published software images and cryptographic attestation. Extends device security model to cloud AI.
sources.claims_weakened: Apple's own description; no independent audit of PCC claims was located in this research.

sources.title: Apple Intelligence Foundation Language Models - Apple Machine Learning Research
sources.claims: Apple's foundation models: ~3B-parameter on-device model optimised for Apple silicon (KV-cache sharing, 2-bit quantisation-aware training in the 2025 tech report) and a larger server model on Private Cloud Compute built on Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts. Published AFM tech reports July 2024 and July 2025.
sources.claims_weakened: Shows Apple's disclosed model sizes are far below frontier cloud models; the architecture is optimisation-led, not frontier-scale.

sources.title: Adding server-side intelligence with Private Cloud Compute - Apple Developer Documentation
sources.claims: Apple Developer Foundation Models framework gives apps access to the on-device model and to the server model through Private Cloud Compute, which offers a 32K-token context window and stronger capability than the on-device model.
sources.claims_weakened: A 32K-token context is small versus frontier cloud models, a technical limit on what PCC can do.

sources.title: Apple A19 Pro - Benchmarks & Specs - CPU Monkey
sources.claims: A19 Pro (iPhone 17 Pro / 17 Pro Max, iPhone Air) launched September 2025 on TSMC third-generation 3nm (N3P); 6-core CPU with 2 performance cores up to 4.26 GHz and 4 efficiency cores; 5- or 6-core GPU variants.
sources.claims_weakened: Confirms the A19 generation was still 3nm, so the 2nm step arrives only with A20 in 2026.

sources.title: A20 Pro Explained: Inside Apple's First 2nm iPhone Chip
sources.claims: A20 Pro is Apple's first 2nm iPhone chip on TSMC N2 (GAAFET nanosheets), 6-core CPU, 7-core GPU, dual 16-core Neural Engine (32 cores) said to double AI throughput versus A19 Pro and rated around 52 TOPS; N2 wafers about $30,000 versus $18,000-20,000 for 3nm.
sources.claims_weakened: The 52 TOPS and wafer-price figures are trade-press estimates, not Apple or TSMC disclosure; they are used as directional indicators only.

sources.title: IDC: Smartphone shipments set for record 16.7% drop in 2026 as memory crisis hits full force
sources.claims: Worldwide smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1bn units, steepest annual contraction on record, while total market value grows 6.3% to $613bn; ASP $581 in 2026, +27.6% YoY, revised up from $550; NAND/DRAM costs up over 300% YoY and rising until at least 2028; Android shipments -24.3% and Android share down ~7pp while iOS share rises almost 4pp to a record 23.6% with Apple shipments down only 1.3%; HarmonyOS nearly triples to 51m units in 2026; foldables +12.6% to 22.9m units in 2026 and +18% to ~27m in 2027, with Apple shipping more than 17m foldable iPhones by 2027 (~40% of the category, ASP above $2,550, $45.7bn of value); sub-$100 segment of 173m units in 2025 down almost 60% in Q2 2026; emerging markets down over 20% in 2026.
sources.claims_weakened: The earlier IDC forecast of a 13.9% decline to 1.09bn units and $550 ASP (issued one quarter earlier), and the HarmonyOS 62m-unit figure in that earlier release; shows how fast third-party estimates are moving.

sources.title: Google's courtroom victory just saved Apple from a big headache (CNN Business)
sources.claims: Judge Amit Mehta's 2025-09-02 remedy order in US v. Google bars exclusive default-search agreements but permits Google to keep paying partners to distribute search; Apple can continue receiving the payments (estimated at $20bn in 2022); Eddy Cue testified Google search queries on Apple devices fell for the first time in April 2025; Gartner estimated search volume could fall 25% by 2026 as users move to AI tools.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens the view that the 2025 remedies extinguished Apple's search-licensing revenue; also weakens the durability case, since query decline and AI substitution threaten the revenue base the payment is calculated on.

sources.title: Google's Payments to Apple Reached $20 Billion in 2022, Cue Says (Bloomberg)
sources.claims: Alphabet paid Apple $20bn in 2022 for Google to be the default search engine in Safari, per newly unsealed court documents in the US DOJ antitrust case; the figure was given in testimony by Apple services chief Eddy Cue.
sources.claims_weakened: Shows the scale of the search-licensing revenue inside Apple's Services line; Apple itself does not disclose the amount, so the $20bn is a 2022 court-record figure, not a current company disclosure.

sources.title: Press Release No 96/26 - General Court dismisses Apple's actions on gatekeeper designation
sources.claims: General Court judgment 2026-07-08 (Joined Cases T-1079/23, T-1080/23, T-214/24) dismissed Apple's actions against its DMA gatekeeper designation for the App Store and iOS; iMessage actions inadmissible. Apple's legal route to narrow DMA obligations in the EU is closed at first instance, appeal limited to points of law within two months and ten days.
sources.claims_weakened: Removes the option that Apple could litigate its way out of DMA interoperability and anti-steering duties.

sources.title: Commission finds Apple and Meta in breach of the Digital Markets Act (IP/25/1085)
sources.claims: European Commission fined Apple EUR 500 million on 2025-04-23 for breaching the DMA anti-steering obligation in the App Store, ordering Apple to remove technical and commercial restrictions on steering and to refrain from equivalent conduct; fines can reach 10% of global annual turnover and periodic penalties apply for non-compliance after 60 days. First DMA non-compliance decision.
sources.claims_weakened: Corrects secondary reporting that dated the EUR 500m fine to April 2026; the decision is 2025-04-23.

sources.title: Apple Kills Old Siri, Replaces It With Google Gemini 2026
sources.claims: Siri rebuild timeline: Phase 1 in iOS 26.4 (spring 2026) added on-screen awareness, contextual understanding and cross-app actions; Phase 2 in iOS 27 (September 2026) added conversational multi-turn dialogue, multi-app automation and the option to use third-party App Store AI models as Siri's engine. Reports Apple pays Google about $1bn a year for the Gemini licence on top of a roughly $20bn a year default-search payment. Device support starts at iPhone 15 Pro.
sources.claims_weakened: Blog-level sourcing for the $1bn licence fee and the claim that Google servers perform the inference; both conflict with Apple's statement that Apple Intelligence runs on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute.

sources.title: Apple Vision Pro Sales 2026: 390K to 45K a Quarter, Data
sources.claims: Vision Pro shipments: about 390,000 units in 2024 (IDC estimate cited by the Financial Times, January 2026); only about 45,000 units in Q4 2025 after the M5 Vision Pro launched in October 2025; lifetime shipments around 600,000; IDC forecasts about 290,000 units in 2026 and about $636m of revenue, with a lower-cost model planned for late 2026 aimed at enterprise and education.
sources.claims_weakened: Shows the spatial computing line is a sub-1% revenue business, undermining Vision Pro as a growth pillar.

sources.title: Apple buys Israeli startup Q.ai as the AI race heats up
sources.claims: Apple acquired Israeli AI-audio startup Q.ai, confirmed 2026-01-29; the Financial Times reported a value near $2bn, which would make it Apple's second-largest acquisition after Beats ($3bn, 2014). Apple did not disclose terms.
sources.claims_weakened: Price is press-reported, not confirmed by Apple; Q.ai's technology is not publicly described in detail.

sources.title: Apple iPhone production in India hits 25% of global output
sources.claims: Apple iPhone production in India rose 53% in 2025 to about 55 million units, roughly a quarter of global iPhone output, according to Bloomberg; Foxconn and Tata expanded capacity.
sources.claims_weakened: Page returned HTTP 502 on fetch; figures are taken from the search result summary and were not verified against the full article.

sources.title: Apple in Early Settlement Talks With DOJ Over Antitrust Case
sources.claims: Apple and the US Department of Justice are in early discussions to settle the 2024 antitrust lawsuit alleging Apple violated antitrust law with the iPhone; the case remains unresolved as of 2026.
sources.claims_weakened: Settlement talks are not an outcome; a remedy that opens App Store distribution or default-payment economics would hit Services gross margin.

sources.title: India's share in global iPhone assembly projected to reach 28% in 2026
sources.claims: India's share of global iPhone assembly projected to reach 28% in 2026, with Foxconn and Tata Electronics as assemblers after Tata's acquisition of Wistron's and Pegatron's India operations.
sources.claims_weakened: Projection, not disclosed by Apple; assembly share is not the same as value share or component localisation.

IDC: Global smartphone shipments fall 7.4% in Q2 2026 (top-5 vendor shares)
sources.claims: Global smartphone shipments fell 7.4% YoY to 276.3m units in Q2 2026; Q2 2026 top-5: Samsung 62.7m (22.7%, +8.1%), Apple 55.7m (20.2%, +14.9% on record Q2 shipments), Xiaomi 31.2m (11.3%, -26.4%), OPPO 28.9m (10.5%, -17.1%), vivo 21.2m (7.7%, -19.6%); memory costs up nearly 300% and over 65% of BOM at the low end; Samsung and Apple the only top-5 vendors to grow, lifting share 3.2pp and 3.9pp; Apple on track for a record 22% annual share; Huawei +19.9%.
sources.claims_weakened: Claims of Apple unit-share erosion in the 2026 downturn: Apple gained 3.9pp of global share YoY in Q2 2026 despite a 7.4% market decline.

sources.title: IDC: Worldwide personal computing device market, Q2 2026 performance and 2026 outlook
sources.claims: Worldwide personal computing device shipments (PCs plus tablets) about 103m units in Q2 2026, -6.8% YoY; vendor shares Q2 2026: Lenovo 20.1% (+2.5%), Apple 18.2% (-0.4%), HP 12.7% (-8.9%), Dell 9.1% (-5.1%), Samsung 6.2% (-18.6%); Apple holds 55.3% of detachable tablets; macOS shipments grew 17.4% on MacBook Neo demand while Windows fell 6.7% and Android fell 19.6%; HarmonyOS NEXT reached 1.6%; full-year 2026 forecast about 398m units, -11.3%, with macOS the only major OS forecast to grow (+3.3%); market CAGR 1.5% 2026-2030.
sources.claims_weakened: Claims that Apple is a marginal PC vendor: at 18.2% of PC-plus-tablet units in Q2 2026 it is the number-two vendor, and macOS is the only major OS expected to grow in 2026.

sources.title: IDC: Worldwide wearable device market, Q2 2026 and 2026 outlook
sources.claims: Worldwide wearable device shipments about 148m units in Q2 2026 (+2.7% YoY); Apple leads with 15.5% share (+8.9%), Xiaomi 11.7%, Huawei 10.9%, Samsung 6.8%, Imagine Marketing 4.9%; earwear 64.9% of units and Apple leads earwear with 17.2%; Huawei tops smartwatches with 18.8% ahead of Apple's 17.2%; Meta holds 78.4% of glasses, Oura 67.0% of rings; wearables forecast about 625m units in 2026 (+1.7%) with a 2.4% CAGR to about 687m by 2030; smartwatches -3.7% in 2026 then 1.3% CAGR; glasses +35.2% in 2026.
sources.claims_weakened: Claims that Apple Watch dominates smartwatch units: Huawei leads smartwatch shipments at 18.8% versus Apple at 17.2% in Q2 2026, and Apple's overall wearables lead is 15.5% on AirPods-led earwear, not on watches.

sources.title: IDC: India smartphone market Q1 2026
sources.claims: India smartphone shipments 31.0m units in Q1 2026, -4.1% YoY, while market value rose 5.8%; ASP a record US$302 (+10.4%); sub-$100 segment -59% with share falling from 18% to 8%; US$600-800 band +32% and share 4% to 6%; US$800+ 7% share; top five by units vivo #1, Samsung #2, OPPO #3, Apple #4, Motorola #5; online channel fell 14% and its share slipped from 42% to 38%; India prices expected to rise further through 2027.
sources.claims_weakened: Claims that India is already an Apple volume market: Apple ranks fourth by units in Q1 2026 behind vivo, Samsung and OPPO, in a market where value is growing faster than volume.

sources.title: IDC: PC market enters volatile territory as memory shortage persists through 2027
sources.claims: IDC forecasts global PC shipments -11.3% in 2026 with Q4 2026 down 20% YoY and no memory relief before end-2027; PC ASP growth of 17% in 2026; Apple's MacBook Neo drove stronger-than-expected notebook demand and forced IDC to revise its notebook forecast up, putting "real pressure on the entire PC ecosystem" with vendors expected to respond with new silicon, a more efficient Microsoft OS and aggressive promotional pricing.
sources.claims_weakened: The idea that Apple cannot compete on PC price: the MacBook Neo is described by IDC as pressuring the whole PC ecosystem on price and demand, not as a niche premium product.

sources.claims_weakened: Apple has not published an AI subscription price or tier; the page could not be fetched (HTTP 403) and the claim rests on the search summary. Treat as unverified.

sources.title: StockAnalysis — Samsung Electronics market capitalisation, 2026-10-30

sources.claims_weakened: A won market value converted at the current rate is sensitive to USD/KRW; a second tracker puts the dollar value at $1.105 trillion. Samsung is a memory-cycle beneficiary, so its multiple is not a clean hardware comp for Apple.

sources.title: Clearank — Apple analyst ratings and price-target range, October 2026
sources.claims: As of 2026-10-30, 43 Wall Street analysts cover Apple: 24 buy or strong buy, 13 hold, 6 sell or strong sell, with 12-month price targets from $245.00 to $405.00. The consensus range brackets the 2026-10-30 close of $344.63.
sources.claims_weakened: Does not state a median target; other trackers put the median at $338-$355, so the dispersion is wide (roughly $245-$405) and the sell-side is not unanimous on upside.

sources.title: CompaniesMarketCap — Samsung Electronics P/E and market cap, October 2026
sources.claims: Samsung Electronics traded at a trailing P/E of 12.5x in October 2026 (18.2x at end-2025) and a market capitalisation of about $1.105 trillion, making it the world's 14th most valuable company.
sources.claims_weakened: Samsung's earnings are at a memory-cycle peak, which flatters its P/E and understates its through-cycle multiple; it is not a US GAAP filer, so the SEC XBRL tool returns n/a.

sources.title: Zacks — Apple Q4 FY2026 preview and revenue guidance, October 2026
sources.claims: For fiscal Q4 2026 (September quarter), Apple guided revenue to increase 9-11% year over year; results are scheduled for 2026-11-02. Q4 FY2025 revenue was $102.5 billion, so the guide implies roughly $111.7-113.8 billion.
sources.claims_weakened: Sell-side preview, not Apple's own release; Apple stopped giving a revenue point guide in 2020 and the 9-11% figure may be an analyst aggregation rather than company guidance. The actual Q4 print is due after this report's as-of date.

sources.title: DrawdownTracker — Apple drawdown and recovery history to 2026-10-30
sources.claims: Apple's intra-year peak-to-trough drawdowns: 2018 -36.73% ($58.02 on 2018-10-03 to $36.71 on 2018-12-24, 82 days); 2020 -31.43% ($81.80 on 2020-02-12 to $56.09 on 2020-03-23, 40 days); 2022 -30.75% ($182.01 on 2022-01-03 to $126.04 on 2022-12-28, 359 days); 2025 -30.22% ($247.10 on 2025-02-24 to $172.42 on 2025-04-08, 43 days). Ten-year average intra-year drawdown -21.4% lasting 82 days. Apple closed at $344.63 on 2026-10-30, 1.23% below its all-time-high close of $348.91 on 2026-10-29; the S&P 500 was 3.05% and the Nasdaq-100 9.09% below their highs.
sources.claims_weakened: Calendar-year intra-year draws understate the max historical drawdown (-38.73%, year not specified); prices are split-adjusted closes, and a drawdown is not a valuation signal on its own.

sources.title: AlphaStreet — Apple Q2 FY2026 results and $100bn buyback, April 2026
sources.claims: In late April 2026 Apple reported fiscal Q2 2026 revenue of $111.18 billion and net income of $29.58 billion, raised its quarterly dividend about 4% to $0.27 per share and its board approved a new $100 billion share repurchase authorisation (about 2.4% of market capitalisation at the time).
sources.claims_weakened: A secondary summary of Apple's release; the $100 billion figure and $0.27 dividend are corroborated by the Q3 FY2026 8-K [S13], but the Q2 revenue and net income are not in a filing read for this section.

sources.title: LitigationLogic — Google search default-payment remedy effective June 2026
sources.claims: The prohibition on Google paying device makers to pre-install its search engine as the default took effect in June 2026 under the final remedy order issued by US District Judge Amit Mehta in April 2026; Apple, Samsung and Mozilla must present choice screens. The Apple-Google payment has been reported at about $20 billion a year.
sources.claims_weakened: Other reports say the Apple-Google agreement survives in restricted, non-exclusive form and is under appeal, so the revenue loss is uncertain and Apple does not disclose the amount. A legal blog, not a court record.

sources.title: CNBC: Apple taps John Ternus as CEO to replace Tim Cook, becoming chairman

sources.title: Apple Leadership: Kevan Parekh
sources.claims: Kevan Parekh is Apple's CFO reporting to CEO John Ternus; oversees accounting, business support, FP&A, treasury, investor relations, internal audit, tax and Corporate Services; joined Apple in 2013, previously VP of Financial Planning and Analysis and VP of Worldwide Finance; before Apple held senior roles at Thomson Reuters and General Motors; BS in Electrical Engineering from the University of Michigan and MBA from the University of Chicago.
sources.claims_weakened: Company biography; no years for degrees, no prior CFO title and no disclosure of his CFO pay beyond the proxy.

sources.title: Apple Leadership: Eddy Cue
sources.claims: Eddy Cue is SVP Services and Health, overseeing the App Store, Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple News, Apple Pay, Apple Card, Maps, Apple Ads, iCloud and productivity apps plus health and fitness; joined Apple in 1989 and helped create the Apple Store online (1998), the iTunes Store (2003) and the App Store (2008); bachelor's degree in Computer Science and Economics from Duke University.
sources.claims_weakened: Company biography; no degree year and no disclosure of Services margin responsibility.

sources.title: Apple Leadership: Craig Federighi
sources.claims: Craig Federighi is SVP Software Engineering, oversees iOS, iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS, and also leads Apple's core AI efforts including foundation models, Apple Intelligence and Siri; returned to Apple in 2009 to lead macOS engineering and took on iOS in 2012; previously NeXT, Apple and about a decade at Ariba including CTO; MS in Computer Science and BS in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from UC Berkeley.
sources.claims_weakened: Company biography; no years for degrees, no evidence on AI delivery timelines.

sources.title: Apple Newsroom: John Giannandrea to retire from Apple; Amar Subramanya joins as VP of AI
sources.claims: On 2025-12-01 Apple announced John Giannandrea, SVP Machine Learning and AI Strategy, was stepping down to serve as an adviser before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya joined as VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, leading Apple Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety and evaluation; Subramanya was most recently corporate VP of AI at Microsoft and spent 16 years at Google, where he was head of engineering for Google's Gemini Assistant; the balance of Giannandrea's organisation moved to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue; Federighi oversees the work to bring a more personalised Siri to users in 2026.
sources.claims_weakened: Company framing of a planned change; confirms an AI leadership disruption, an external hire and Siri's slip to 2026.

sources.title: Apple Leadership: Johny Srouji
sources.claims: Johny Srouji is Apple's chief hardware officer overseeing product design, system engineering, reliability testing and technologies including Apple silicon, cellular, displays, cameras, sensors and batteries; joined Apple in 2008 to lead iPhone application processors; previously held senior positions at Intel and IBM; bachelor's and master's degrees in Computer Science from Technion.
sources.claims_weakened: Company biography; no years for degrees and no disclosure of succession depth beneath him in silicon.

sources.title: Apple Leadership: Deirdre O'Brien

sources.claims_weakened: Company biography; no degree years and no disclosure of retail revenue or headcount metrics.

sources.title: CNBC: Apple picks Google's Gemini to run AI-powered Siri coming this year
sources.claims: On 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced a multiyear partnership under which Apple will lean on Google's Gemini models to power Apple's AI features, including a major Siri upgrade expected later in 2026.
sources.claims_weakened: Does not disclose financial terms; confirms Apple is dependent on a competitor's frontier model for its flagship assistant.

sources.title: European Commission press release IP/16/2923: State aid - Ireland gave illegal tax benefits to Apple worth up to €13 billion
sources.claims: On 2016-08-30 the European Commission decided that Ireland granted illegal state aid worth up to €13 billion to Apple through 1991 and 2007 tax rulings concerning Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe, and ordered recovery of the unpaid taxes for 2003-2014.
sources.claims_weakened: The Commission's own finding, later annulled by the General Court in 2020 before the ECJ reinstated it in 2024; the amount is an estimate of unpaid tax plus interest.

sources.title: Clifford Chance: The EU's €13 billion Apple tax recovery order
sources.claims: Apple had two entities incorporated in Ireland, Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe, each with an Irish branch taxable in Ireland and a head office not subject to Irish tax; the entities held the intellectual property rights to manufacture and sell Apple products outside the Americas under a cost-sharing agreement with Apple Inc.
sources.claims_weakened: Law-firm briefing on the 2016 Commission decision; describes the pre-2015 structure, not Apple's current Irish entity roles.

sources.title: CNBC: Apple stock split announced
sources.claims: Apple's board approved a four-for-one stock split, announced with fiscal third-quarter 2020 results on 2020-07-30.
sources.claims_weakened: Announcement only; does not give the effective date or the split history.

sources.title: Strasmore: Apple stock split history and ratios
sources.claims: Apple's four-for-one stock split took effect on 2020-08-31; it was the fifth split in the company's history, one pre-split share now equalling 56 shares after all splits.
sources.claims_weakened: Secondary blog compilation; does not reconcile the exact split-adjusted prices.

sources.title: MacRumors: Apple Reaches 2.5 Billion Active Devices (2026-01-29)
sources.claims: Apple announced on 2026-01-29 that its installed base exceeded 2.5 billion active devices, up from more than 2.35 billion a year earlier, quoting Tim Cook; supports the Services attach and upgrade-pool argument.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens the 2.3 billion installed-base figure and any statement that Apple discloses no device count; Apple still discloses no replacement rate or device mix.

sources.title: TrendForce: Diverging Memory Market Outlook in 2027 as DRAM Supply Remains Tight While NAND Flash Supply Conditions Ease
sources.claims: DRAM sufficiency ratio -1% to -2% in 2026 and the supply-demand gap widens in 2027; new DRAM capacity ramps meaningfully only in 2H27 with substantial output not until 2028; consumer electronics including smartphones and notebooks stay under pressure with another year of declining shipments in 2027; NAND loosens in 2H27.
sources.claims_weakened: The base case that memory normalises around 2028 and that gross margin gives back only about one point in FY2027; IDC's 2028 normalisation timing is consistent for DRAM but leaves FY2027 exposed.

sources.title: CNBC: Apple shares downgraded due to memory chip inflation
sources.claims: Phillip Capital cut Apple to reduce on 2026-08-04 with a $290 target, citing memory inflation as a major margin headwind; management expects memory prices to keep rising in 4Q26 and beyond; carry-in inventory, mix and non-memory costs offset it only for a time; DRAM has three suppliers, leaving little sourcing flexibility; Apple fell nearly 10% after the 2026-07-30 results on weak guidance tied to the chip crunch; Apple had already raised iPad and Mac prices.
sources.claims_weakened: The base case that the FY2026 margin give-back is about one point and self-correcting; the assumption that Apple can absorb memory inflation without demand loss.

sources.title: Pip Theory: Apple Q4 FY2026 earnings preview — 47-48% margin guided, inventory doubled
sources.claims: Apple guided fiscal Q4 2026 revenue growth of 9-11% (about $111.7-113.7bn) and gross margin of 47-48% including about 1 point of tariff refunds, i.e. roughly 46-47% ex-refunds against 48.1% ex-refund in the June quarter; consensus about $113.3bn revenue and $1.99 EPS; carry-in inventory benefit said to fade after September; Cook called the memory environment a once-in-a-century flood; CFO Parekh said the memory cost increase was larger than the entire fall in gross margin from June to the September guide.
sources.claims_weakened: Any reading of the 50.1% June-quarter margin as a new floor: Apple's own September guide implies a 2.1-3.1 point sequential decline and a lower underlying margin than a year earlier.

sources.title: TechNode: Huawei grows as China's smartphone shipments fall 15.4% in Q3 2026 (IDC)
sources.claims: IDC preliminary data reported 2026-10-13: China smartphone shipments fell 15.4% year on year to 57.9m units in Q3 2026, a sixth straight quarterly decline; Apple shipments fell 4.3% but its share rose to 17.8% from 15.8%; Huawei was the only major vendor with double-digit growth, shipping 12.2m units for about 21% share.
sources.claims_weakened: The read that Apple's 30% Greater China revenue growth reflects durable share gains rather than a shrinking-market mix effect; it also shows China volume falling under the June-quarter run rate.

sources.title: Law360: DOJ, Google want D.C. Circuit priority for search appeal
sources.claims: The DOJ and Google jointly asked the D.C. Circuit to give their cross-appeals priority so that oral argument could be scheduled as soon as 2026-12-09 in the search monopolization remedies appeal.
sources.claims_weakened: The assumption that the Google search-payment risk is a 2027-2028 tail: argument is set for December 2026, so a ruling on whether distribution payments can be barred outright is plausible within the twelve-month window.

sources.title: Invezz: Apple stock falls after Jefferies downgrade to Underperform, $263.66 target
sources.claims: Jefferies cut Apple to Underperform on 2026-08-10 and lowered its price target to $263.66 from $285.56, citing rising memory costs, a weakening premium iPhone roadmap and underwhelming AI monetisation.
sources.claims_weakened: The base case fair value of $296: an independent sell-side bear case lands about 11% below it and close to a margin-cut earnings base at a normal multiple.

sources.title: Computerworld: How Satya Nadella navigated Microsoft to $3 trillion market value
sources.claims: Microsoft's market value rose from about $381 billion in early 2014, when Nadella became CEO, to about $3 trillion a decade later, as the cloud transition replaced declining PC-licence revenue; much of the return came from re-rating a low starting multiple as well as earnings growth.
sources.claims_weakened: Cautions against reading a successful incumbent transition as repeatable at a 39.5x starting multiple: Microsoft began near 10-12x earnings, so its rerating had room that Apple's does not.

sources.title: 9to5Mac: Apple sets Q4 2026 earnings release for November 2
sources.claims: Apple guided fiscal Q4 2026 gross margin of 47%-48%, down from 50.1% in the June 2026 quarter, which included a roughly two-percentage-point benefit from tariff refunds; results scheduled for 2026-11-02.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens any assumption that the 50.1% June-quarter gross margin is a floor: the company's own guide implies a 2-3 point decline including one point of refunds.

sources.title: The curse of agility: the Nokia Corporation and the loss of market dominance in mobile phones, 2003-2013
sources.claims: Nokia held roughly 40-50% of global mobile phone share in 2007 and fell below 5% by 2013 as the smartphone platform shift moved value to software ecosystems it did not control; the decline took about six years from the iPhone launch to the sale of the devices business.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens any view that device leadership is durable through a platform shift; supports pricing the AI interface shift as a real risk even for a share leader.

sources.title: AppleInsider: Jefferies cuts AAPL target to $263.66, downgrades to underperform
sources.claims: Jefferies downgraded Apple to underperform on 2026-08-10 and cut its price target to $263.66 from $285.56, citing supply-chain checks that the all-glass anniversary iPhone had been cancelled and rising memory costs; the target implied about 16% downside from the then-price.
sources.claims_weakened: Provides an independent sell-side anchor near the margin-adjusted base value of about $268, against a consensus target of $339.35.

rows.finding: A20 Pro (iPhone 18 generation, September 2026) is Apple's first 2nm phone chip on TSMC N2 with a dual 16-core Neural Engine and about 52 TOPS, roughly double the A19 Pro's AI throughput; the A19 Pro (September 2025) was still TSMC N3P at up to 4.26 GHz.
rows.mechanism: Denser logic per watt is what lets a phone run a multi-billion-parameter model inside a thermal envelope, so node leadership translates directly into on-device AI capability and battery life; but N2 wafers at about $30,000 versus $18,000-20,000 for 3nm raise silicon cost per unit.
rows.benchmark: A19 Pro on N3P (2025) and 3nm wafer pricing of $18,000-20,000; product gross margin 39.9% for the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier.
rows.weakens: TOPS and wafer prices are trade-press estimates, not Apple or TSMC disclosure; N2 is TSMC's process, available to Qualcomm, MediaTek and others, so the node advantage is rented from a supplier, not owned.
rows.implication: Silicon leadership is real but compresses margin as node costs rise; price the iPhone gross margin at risk of memory and wafer inflation rather than assuming AI drives ASP up.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What is the actual A20 Pro die cost and yield, and how much of the N2 premium does Apple absorb versus pass through in the $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro price?

rows.finding: Apple's C2 modem ships in the iPhone 18 Pro and the foldable iPhone Duo with US mmWave bands and 15% lower energy use than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem.
rows.mechanism: In-house modem design removes a $10-20 class royalty and a supplier's margin from the bill of materials and improves cellular-to-OS integration, but a partial roll-out leaves Qualcomm with leverage over the highest-ASP SKU and over certification risk.
rows.benchmark: Qualcomm remains the modem in the iPhone 18 Pro Max; the C1 debuted in the low-cost iPhone 16e, so the substitution has taken two generations to reach flagship tier.
rows.weakens: The split may reflect mmWave certification, supply or performance risk rather than a deliberate strategy, which would mean the technical gap is not yet closed.
rows.implication: Modem integration is a slow but real margin lever; it supports the hardware gross-margin case only if the Pro Max moves to C2 in the 2027 cycle.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Does Apple's FY2026 10-K disclose Qualcomm as a single-source supplier, and what share of iPhone units still carry a Qualcomm modem?

rows.finding: Apple's own foundation models are a ~3B-parameter on-device model (KV-cache sharing, 2-bit quantisation-aware training) and a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts server model on Private Cloud Compute with a 32K-token context; on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced that the next generation of Apple Foundation Models will be based on Google's Gemini models and cloud technology.
rows.mechanism: On-device inference is bounded by memory bandwidth and power, which caps practical model size at single-digit billions of parameters; Apple therefore offloads hard queries to PCC and, from 2026, to Gemini-derived models. Renting the frontier layer cuts training capex but turns model quality into a purchased input with a per-query cost and a supplier who is also a competitor in search and assistants.
rows.benchmark: A 32K-token context against frontier cloud assistants that handle far longer contexts; a ~3B on-device model against server models reported at roughly 8x its size.
rows.weakens: Apple's joint statement says Apple Intelligence continues to run on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute, while trade press reports that Google's cloud performs Gemini inference — the boundary is undisclosed, and with it the true cost and privacy position.
rows.implication: The AI layer is a rented input, not a moat; the investment case must rest on distribution, silicon and privacy orchestration, and on whether Apple can charge for AI through iCloud+ without ceding margin to Google.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Where does Gemini inference physically run, what does Apple pay per query, and does the Google agreement give Apple rights to fine-tune or distil Gemini for on-device use?

rows.finding: The iPhone 18 Pro ($1,199), iPhone 18 Pro Max ($1,299) and the first foldable iPhone Duo ($1,999, on sale 2026-10-23) extend the range upward; iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and Greater China rose 30% to $64.8bn.
rows.mechanism: A foldable at $1,999 tests whether Apple can still create a new hardware price tier; the China rebound shows the installed base still converts when the product cycle is strong, which funds services and buybacks.
rows.benchmark: Vision Pro's $3,499 launch produced about 390,000 units in its first year and about 45,000 in Q4 2025 — the base rate for a new Apple category at a super-premium price.
rows.weakens: The Duo arrives roughly seven years after Samsung's first foldable, so Apple is following, not leading; and the 22% iPhone growth is against a weak prior year and helped by tariff refunds and currency.
rows.implication: The product cycle supports FY2027 revenue but does not prove AI differentiation; treat the foldable as an ASP lever with unproven volume.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What first-weekend Duo orders and return rates look like, and whether the $1,999 price holds without carrier subsidy.

rows.finding: Apple's health stack is a sequence of FDA-cleared features rather than one device: Hypertension Notification Feature (K250507, cleared 2025-09-11), Sleep Apnea Notification Feature (K240929, 2024-09-13), Hearing Aid Feature De Novo (DEN230081, 2024-09-12) and a Medical Imaging Calibration Feature (K253582, 2026-04-01), on top of ECG (2020) and atrial fibrillation history (2022).
rows.mechanism: Each clearance requires its own clinical validation and quality system, so a competitor must replicate the evidence file feature by feature; that turns sensor hardware into a regulated, slow-moving moat and creates a credible path to reimbursed health services.
rows.benchmark: Twelve FDA device records naming Apple as applicant since 2020, six of them in the last 24 months; no competitor in the retrieved records matches that cadence in consumer wearables.
rows.weakens: These are notification and screening features, not diagnoses; none carries Medicare reimbursement in the retrieved records, and the Medical Imaging Calibration clearance's commercial use is not disclosed.
rows.implication: Health is the most defensible part of the product portfolio and the most plausible route to a paid health subscription; it deserves a separate valuation line from hardware.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Which of these features are cleared in China and the EU, and does Apple have a reimbursement or insurer partnership for hypertension notifications?

rows.finding: Apple does not disclose a patent count; the FY2025 10-K states only that it is 'pursuing thousands of applications around the world' and holds a broad portfolio of patents, designs, copyrights and trade secrets, and that no single right protects its products.
rows.mechanism: A diffuse portfolio with no blocking single right supports freedom to operate but gives little measurable exclusion power in AI, where training data and model weights rather than patents decide capability; the enforceable assets are design, silicon know-how and trade secrets.
rows.benchmark: Peer comparison on patent counts could not be completed: USPTO Patent Center and EPO Espacenet were not searchable in this run, so a quantitative portfolio comparison is missing.
rows.weakens: Without counts, grants and citation data, any claim that Apple's patent moat is strong or weak is unquantified; the 10-K's 'thousands' language is the only primary datum.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a patent-based moat; underwrite manufacturing know-how, regulatory clearances and installed base, and request a patent-landscape export before relying on IP as a differentiator.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Can a USPTO Patent Center and Espacenet export for Apple's 2024-2026 AI, health-sensing, foldable and AR filings be obtained to test grant rates and citation depth?

plan.decision_question: Is Apple's silicon-plus-OS integration still a durable technical advantage in the AI era, or is Apple becoming a fast-follower that licenses others' frontier models?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack in the industry, but in 2026 the company formally rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not AI leadership.
plan.why_different: This section judges the technology itself: what is proven, at what performance, under what dependency, and how long a funded competitor would need — not the market size, the unit economics or the valuation, which belong to other sections.
plan.mechanism: Owning the SoC, modem, wireless chip and OS lets Apple put a ~3B-parameter model on more than two billion devices at near-zero marginal cost and keep orchestration and privacy; licensing Gemini removes the frontier-training cost but converts model capability into a per-query input cost and a Google dependency, so value shifts from model ownership to distribution and to regulated features that competitors cannot copy without their own trials and FDA clearances.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own prior generation (A19 Pro on TSMC N3P, 2025) and 3nm wafer economics; Qualcomm as the incumbent modem supplier still in the iPhone 18 Pro Max; Samsung and Huawei as foldable and on-device-AI incumbents; Google as the model supplier and would-be competitor; Vision Pro against the scale needed for a platform (sub-1% of revenue).
plan.counter_evidence: Siri's multi-year delivery failure forced Apple to license Gemini (2026-01-12) on reported ~$1bn a year; on-device models are ~3B parameters with a 32K context, far below frontier cloud models; Vision Pro shipped only ~45,000 units in Q4 2025; the C2 modem still does not cover the largest Pro Max SKU; and Apple publishes no patent count, so the IP moat cannot be quantified from primary sources.
plan.visual: Technology comparison table plus product inventory and patent/IP table; the FDA clearance table carries the health-moat argument.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, world-class, best-in-class, about 5, many patents, recently, industry-leading (as an assertion)

rows.finding: In FY2025 Services produced $82,314M of gross profit on $109,158M of revenue (75.4% margin), 42.2% of Apple's $195,201M total gross profit from 26.2% of revenue; Services gross profit per $1 of Products gross profit rose from $0.55 in FY2023 to $0.73 in FY2025.
rows.mechanism: The installed base is an annuity: a device sold at a 36-38% product margin carries a stream of services at 71-76% margin whose incremental cost is close to nil, so each hardware dollar underwrites a growing high-margin attach.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own FY2023 mix (Services 22.2% of revenue, 35.7% of gross profit) and Microsoft's 67.9% FY2026 gross margin, which is a pure software mix rather than a hardware-plus-attach mix.
rows.weakens: Services gross margin is flat year on year at 75.6% in Q3 FY2026, so the attach is not itself becoming more profitable; the mix gain comes from revenue share, not margin rate.
rows.implication: The mix-shift thesis is real at the gross-profit level and is the single best explanation for the re-rating; it argues for paying for durability of attach rather than for device growth.
rows.confidence: high - audited segment and category data in the FY2025 10-K
rows.follow_up: What share of Services gross profit comes from third-party licensing (Google) versus Apple's own subscriptions, and does Apple disclose App Store revenue?

rows.finding: The mix shift reversed in FY2026: over the nine months to 2026-06-27 Products gross profit grew 26.3% ($108,819M vs $86,190M) while Services gross profit grew 15.3% ($69,963M vs $60,670M), so Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit from 42.2% in FY2025.
rows.mechanism: Products gross margin jumped to 39.9% in 9M FY2026 and 40.1% in Q3 from 34.5% a year earlier, which Apple attributes to 'a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory'. Hardware margin expansion, not services mix, drove FY2026 gross profit.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 Products gross margin of 36.8% and FY2024's 37.2%; the 3.1-point nine-month gain is the largest in the three-year record and part of it is a tariff-refund credit rather than trading.
rows.weakens: The prevailing narrative that Apple's margin expansion is services-led. In FY2026 it was hardware-led and partly one-off, so the durability of the current 50.1% total gross margin is weaker than the Services share implies.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise the FY2026 gross margin as structural; normalise products gross margin toward the high 30s before valuing, and treat the refund as non-recurring.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on how much of the margin gain is refund versus mix, which Apple does not split
rows.follow_up: How large was the tariff refund recognised in products cost of sales, and when does the Section 232 semiconductor investigation resolve?

rows.finding: Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution and concedes in its FY2025 10-K that a reversal of the 2025-09-02 D.C. District Court remedies order on appeal 'could result in imposition of certain remedies initially proposed by the DOJ, such as those prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution'; the payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents. Apple does not disclose the current amount.
rows.mechanism: Google pays for default placement because Apple's base produces high-value search queries; the payment is booked inside Services advertising at near-100% incremental margin, so its loss would hit Services gross profit disproportionately to revenue.
rows.benchmark: $20bn in 2022 equals 18.3% of Apple's FY2025 Services revenue of $109,158M and 24.3% of FY2025 Services gross profit of $82,314M, on a two-year-old figure that Apple has never confirmed.
rows.weakens: Apple's Services revenue is often described as diversified; on these figures a single counterparty's litigation outcome sits inside the fastest-growing line, and Eddy Cue testified that Google queries on Apple devices fell for the first time in April 2025.
rows.implication: A regulatory hit to services profit is a live, priced risk rather than a tail; it argues for a discount to the multiple, and for asking what the replacement economics are in an AI-search world.
rows.confidence: high on the legal timetable and Apple's own risk language; medium on the dollar amount, which is a 2022 court-record figure and not a company disclosure
rows.follow_up: What is the current annual payment, what is its term, and has Apple disclosed any replacement search partner or AI-answer deal?

rows.finding: App Store revenue is recognised net: Apple records 'only the commission it retains' for third-party app sales, and it is currently subject to a US court order 'preventing it from imposing any commission or fee on certain purchases that consumers make', although the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to allow a commission.
rows.mechanism: Because the commission is recognised gross in Services revenue at close to zero cost, any take-rate compression passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost reduction; the same is true of every euro of DMA-driven alternative distribution in the EU.
rows.benchmark: The DMA already forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures in the EU; Apple states its compliance plan 'has been challenged by the Commission' and that non-compliance carries significant fines.
rows.weakens: Apple does not disclose App Store revenue, the commission rate, or the EU share of it, so the size of the exposure cannot be calculated from filings - it can only be bounded by the Services line.
rows.implication: Treat a structural take-rate cut as a permanent margin haircut to Services rather than a one-off; size it from total Services gross profit of $82,314M in FY2025.
rows.confidence: high - Apple's own risk-factor language
rows.follow_up: What proportion of Services revenue is App Store commission, and how much of that is EU-billed? Apple's Developer Program fee schedule would settle the current rate.

rows.finding: During 2025, 60% of Apple's net sales went through indirect channels (carriers and resellers) and 40% through its own retail and online stores, while SG&A was $27,601M, or 6.6% of revenue.
rows.mechanism: Carriers carry a large part of device acquisition cost through subsidies and instalment plans, so Apple's own selling cost stays near 7% of revenue while a competitor selling direct would carry retail, marketing and channel margin itself - a structural CAC advantage that is not visible in a unit-economics waterfall.
rows.benchmark: SG&A at 6.6% of revenue versus R&D at 8.3%; and versus a telecom-carrier distribution model in which the carrier subsidises the handset to sell a contract.
rows.weakens: Unit economics per device, LTV and LTV:CAC cannot be computed from Apple's disclosure at all, so any per-device table in this report is an approximation and is labelled as such.
rows.implication: The 40/60 direct/indirect split is the reason Apple's margins survive at scale; it also means a carrier-driven demand shock (subsidy withdrawal, eSIM-led direct sales) moves volumes faster than Apple's cost base.
rows.confidence: high on the split; low on translating it into a per-customer CAC, because Apple discloses no unit volumes, no ASP and no marketing line
rows.follow_up: What share of iPhone sales in the US is carrier-financed, and how is the shift to eSIM-only devices changing the carrier/Apple revenue split?

rows.finding: Apple states that future gross margins 'will be subject to volatility and downward pressure', and its Q3 FY2026 10-Q warns of 'a period of supply constraints and increasing costs for components ... including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND) and memory (DRAM)' and that it 'expects these trends to intensify' and 'may materially negatively impact' gross margin.
rows.mechanism: Apple's hardware gross margin is a residual of component pricing against a fixed price ladder; when DRAM and NAND inflate, Apple either absorbs the cost or raises prices into a price-sensitive consumer, so the 39.9% products margin is the peak of a cycle rather than a floor.
rows.benchmark: Products gross margin of 36.8% in FY2025, 37.2% in FY2024 and 36.5% in FY2023 - a three-year band of 0.7 points that the FY2026 39.9% now sits 3.1 points above.
rows.weakens: Any valuation that holds the FY2026 gross margin or operating margin constant; also weakens the case that Apple's pricing power fully offsets input inflation.
rows.implication: Model a gross margin give-back of 1.5-3 points in FY2027 as the memory cycle bites, which on FY2026 TTM revenue of $466,823M is $7-14bn of gross profit before any offset.
rows.confidence: high - the company itself names the mechanism
rows.follow_up: How much of FY2026 memory cost inflation has already been passed through in price, and what is the contract length on DRAM/NAND supply?

rows.finding: Apple converted 1.06x of trailing-twelve-month net income into free cash flow to 2026-06-27 ($136,683M free cash flow on $128,930M net income) with capex at 2.2% of revenue, against Microsoft at 0.50x and 34.9% capex/revenue in FY2026, Alphabet at 0.55x and 22.7% in FY2025 and Meta at 0.76x and 34.7% in FY2025.
rows.mechanism: Apple outsources wafer fabrication and final assembly to TSMC and Foxconn, so the industry's capital intensity sits on suppliers' balance sheets; Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta own their datacentres and are now spending a third of revenue on AI compute, which is why their cash conversion has fallen.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft FY2026 capex $115,948M on $331,839M revenue; Alphabet FY2025 capex $91,447M on $402,836M; Meta FY2025 capex $69,691M on $200,966M.
rows.weakens: The assumption that Apple's capital-light model is unambiguously superior: it also means Apple is buying AI capability through R&D expense (up 32% year on year to $11,729M in Q3 FY2026) rather than owning compute, and may be under-invested relative to peers if AI inference becomes the core platform.
rows.implication: Apple's cash conversion is the best in the peer set and supports the multiple; the offsetting risk is that the peers' capex is building a capability Apple is renting.
rows.confidence: high - all four from their own filings
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's own AI compute arrangement and cost, given R&D is up 33% in nine months to $34,035M?

plan.decision_question: How does Apple convert a hardware installed base into services profit, and how durable is that mix shift through the Google remedies, the DMA and Epic, and a memory-cost cycle?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin on top - every dollar of product gross profit now carries 73 cents of services gross profit - but the mix shift that the multiple pays for stalled in FY2026, when hardware margins helped by tariff refunds grew gross profit twice as fast as Services.
plan.why_different: This section owns the revenue model and the per-unit economics - who pays, for what, and at what margin; the financial statements and their quality sit in the financials section, and share and competitor behaviour sit in the competitive landscape.
plan.mechanism: A device sold at a 37-40% product gross margin carries a stream of services at 71-76% gross margin whose incremental cost is near zero; the attach is funded by 60% indirect distribution in which carriers absorb acquisition cost, and the highest-margin layer of Services is a single counterparty's licensing payment.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own FY2023-FY2025 progression, and Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta on gross margin, capex intensity and cash conversion; telecom-carrier distribution as the channel benchmark.
plan.counter_evidence: FY2026 products gross profit grew 26.3% versus Services at 15.3%, so the mix shift reversed; the Google payment depends on an appeal Apple says could remove it; the App Store commission is under a court order and DMA-mandated alternative fees; and memory and NAND costs are rising with the company warning margins face downward pressure.
plan.visual: The unit-economics waterfall per $1,000 of revenue by line, plus a pricing-and-mix table showing what each line earns and the disclosed price/mix driver.
plan.prohibited: banned_empty_phrases: 'strong ecosystem', 'sticky ecosystem', 'seamless ecosystem', 'high barriers to entry', 'wide moat', 'strong brand', 'well positioned', 'huge installed base', 'services flywheel', 'clear business model'; banned_vagueness: 'many users', 'billions of devices' without a date and a source, 'about $20bn' without a period; no unlabelled per-device figures.

rows.finding: Services reached $109.2bn in FY2025 (26% of $416.2bn revenue) and $91.7bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 14%, with growth attributed to advertising and cloud services; services gross margin was 76.3% against 39.9% for products.
rows.mechanism: Each incremental services dollar carries about 76 cents of gross profit, so a services-led mix shift lifts total gross margin even while memory and N2 wafer costs push product gross margin down; services revenue depends on installed-base monetisation rather than unit growth.
rows.benchmark: FY2025: Services 26% of revenue and 36% of gross profit; 9M FY2026: 25% of revenue and 39% of gross profit; total gross margin 49.1% versus 46.8%.
rows.weakens: Services growth has slowed from 14% (9M FY2026) versus the prior year's pace, and the largest components are exposed to DMA and DOJ remedies.
rows.implication: Services mix, not AI, is the reliable margin engine; value the company on services gross profit compounding at low-to-mid teens and treat any acceleration as upside, not base case.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What share of services growth is advertising versus App Store commission, and how much of advertising is Apple's own inventory versus the Google default-search payment?

rows.finding: R&D rose 33% to $34.0bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27 from $25.7bn, driven by infrastructure costs including AI investments and headcount, while Siri AI shipped in the iOS 27 cycle announced in Q3 FY2026 and Apple has disclosed no AI-specific revenue.
rows.mechanism: Apple funds AI as R&D and data-centre infrastructure rather than as a separate product, so its return appears only indirectly through upgrade rates and services attach; the absence of a price point means the investment is a defensive cost until monetised.
rows.benchmark: R&D $34.6bn in FY2025 (8.3% of sales), $31.4bn in FY2024 and $29.9bn in FY2023; Q3 FY2026 R&D was 11% of sales.
rows.weakens: The iCloud+ gating plan is reported, not announced: Apple has published no AI subscription price, so the monetisation route is unverified.
rows.implication: AI is currently a cost line: the burden is to show it lifts iPhone upgrade rates or services ARPU within two cycles, or it dilutes operating margin.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does Apple disclose the split of AI infrastructure spend between capex, opex and payments to Google, and does the FY2026 10-K quantify the Gemini licence?

rows.finding: iPhone production in India rose 53% in 2025 to about 55 million units, roughly a quarter of global output, with India's share projected at 28% in 2026 and Tata Electronics overtaking Foxconn in export assembly.
rows.mechanism: Moving final assembly to India reduces exposure to US tariffs on China and diversifies single-country risk, but assembly captures a small share of value, so the benefit shows up as avoided cost rather than higher revenue.
rows.benchmark: India about 25% of global iPhone output in 2025 and a projected 28% in 2026, versus a negligible share in 2020.
rows.weakens: Assembly share is not value share; component localisation remains low and the figures are third-party estimates that Apple does not confirm.
rows.implication: India is a tariff-risk hedge rather than a margin driver; it supports the hardware gross-margin floor but does not change the growth algorithm.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What is India's share of iPhone value added and of US-bound units, and what tariff rate applies to Indian-assembled iPhones after the 2026 Section 301 and Section 232 actions?

rows.finding: Apple acquired Q.ai, an Israeli AI-audio start-up, confirmed 2026-01-29 and reported by the Financial Times at close to $2bn, plus the AI data-engineering company Ascend.io, listed by the European Commission with a 2026-06-30 notification.
rows.mechanism: Buying small AI teams converts cash into capability without the integration risk of a large deal; the intangible increase shows the accounting footprint but not yet a product.
rows.benchmark: Prior M&A ceiling: Beats at $3bn (2014); Apple's disclosed intangible assets rose from $11.1bn at 2025-09-27 to $20.3bn at 2026-06-27.
rows.weakens: Q.ai's price is press-reported and its technology is undisclosed; a $2bn deal against $416bn of revenue cannot move the group's growth rate.
rows.implication: M&A posture has shifted from tuck-ins to $2bn-class AI deals, but remains small relative to $146bn of cash and securities: it signals intent, not a change in strategy.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What did Apple actually buy in Q.ai (silent speech, audio AI), and how much of the $9.2bn increase in intangibles is acquisition versus capitalised licences?

rows.finding: The European Commission fined Apple EUR 500m on 2025-04-23 for anti-steering non-compliance, and the EU General Court dismissed Apple's challenge to its gatekeeper designation for the App Store and iOS on 2026-07-08; Apple and the DOJ were reported in 2026 to be in early settlement talks over the 2024 US antitrust case.
rows.mechanism: Both cases attack the rent extracted between developers and users — App Store commission and default-search placement — so a remedy compresses services gross margin directly rather than through a one-off fine.
rows.benchmark: DMA fines can reach 10% of global annual turnover; the EUR 500m fine equals about 0.12% of FY2025 revenue but the remedy, not the fine, is the risk.
rows.weakens: Neither case has produced a final remedy: the DMA fine was for steering, and a DOJ settlement could preserve most of the economics.
rows.implication: Regulatory remedies target the highest-margin services lines; a structural or behavioural remedy should lower the multiple on services rather than on hardware.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What are the terms of any DOJ settlement, and does the DMA interoperability specification extend to the App Store commission structure rather than only to steering?

rows.finding: Vision Pro shipped about 390,000 units in 2024 and about 45,000 in Q4 2025, with IDC forecasting about 290,000 units and $636m of revenue in 2026; Wearables, Home and Accessories grew 2% to $27.3bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27.
rows.mechanism: A platform needs unit volumes to attract developers; at 45,000 units a quarter Vision Pro cannot sustain a developer economy, so its costs stay in R&D while its revenue rounds to nothing at group level.
rows.benchmark: Vision Pro about 600,000 units lifetime versus roughly 55 million iPhones assembled in India alone in 2025; the segment grew only 2% in 9M FY2026.
rows.weakens: Apple does not report Vision Pro units, so all figures are IDC estimates; a cheaper model could change the trajectory.
rows.implication: Spatial computing and home remain option value, not a growth driver; a valuation that capitalises a new-category optionality should discount it heavily.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Is there a lower-cost Vision product in the FY2027 plan, and does Apple report any smart-home device revenue inside the Wearables, Home and Accessories line?

plan.decision_question: Where does Apple's revenue growth come from by FY2028, and is the strategy credible?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's route to FY2028 growth is services mix, a richer iPhone cycle and India, with AI as a retention feature and a possible iCloud+ upsell rather than a revenue line of its own; the plan is credible on cash generation and per-share compounding, but not yet on AI monetisation or on creating a new category.
plan.why_different: This section tests stated and revealed strategy against resources and dates: which milestones must land, which partners carry them, and what the next twelve months must prove. The financial statements themselves and the valuation belong to other sections.
plan.mechanism: Services grow off an installed base that reached a new record, and each incremental services dollar carries about 76 cents of gross profit, so mix shift lifts group margin even when hardware costs rise; AI is funded as R&D and capital expenditure and monetised, if at all, through iCloud+ rather than a new product line; India lowers tariff and concentration risk but captures assembly rather than component value; buybacks convert that cash into per-share growth.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own mix in FY2025 (Services 26% of revenue, 36% of gross profit) versus 9M FY2026 (25% of revenue, 39% of gross profit); R&D intensity 8.3% of FY2025 sales versus 11% in Q3 FY2026; the Beats $3bn deal (2014) as the prior M&A ceiling; the €500m DMA fine as the base rate for regulatory cost; Vision Pro as the base rate for a new-category launch.
plan.counter_evidence: AI features arrived roughly two years after they were first demonstrated, and Siri required a Google licence; the car programme was cancelled and Vision Pro shipped only ~45,000 units in Q4 2025; R&D is up 33% with no disclosed AI revenue; a DOJ settlement or DMA remedy could cut App Store commission and default-search income, which are the highest-margin services lines; and the 2026 growth rate leans on a weak FY2025 comparison, tariff refunds and currency.
plan.visual: Milestone table (Milestone | Target date | Status | What it proves | Source) and partner table (Partner | Scope | Signed | Status | Source); the services-mix and capital-return figures carry the thesis.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, world-class, best-in-class, about 5, many patents, recently, industry-leading (as an assertion), secular growth story

rows.finding: Worldwide smartphone shipments fall 16.7% in 2026 to just over 1bn units while market value rises 6.3% to $613bn and ASP reaches a record $581 (+27.6%), revised up from $550 one quarter earlier; memory costs are up over 300% YoY and rise until at least 2028.
rows.mechanism: AI-server demand diverts NAND/DRAM capacity, raising bill-of-materials for every handset maker; OEMs pass the cost to consumers and cut entry tiers, so the value pool survives while unit volume contracts, and only vendors with early memory contracts and premium mix can hold price.
rows.benchmark: IDC's own prior vintage (13.9% decline, 1.09bn units, $550 ASP) was superseded within one quarter; 173m sub-$100 units shipped in 2025, a segment down almost 60% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: Any unit-volume growth model for Apple, and the assumption that the smartphone market grows with global GDP; also weakens Apple's entry-level reach and emerging-market expansion case.
rows.implication: Judge Apple on value share, ASP and Services attach rather than unit growth; a 1bn-unit market at $581 ASP is a $581bn pool that Apple monetises at roughly twice the industry ASP, so the near-term revenue case does not need market growth.
rows.confidence: high - one primary statistical agency, two vintages, internally consistent (1bn units x $581 = $581bn versus the stated $613bn value, a 5% gap)
rows.follow_up: Does Apple's ASP rise fast enough in FY2027 to offset the unit decline implied by a -16.7% 2026 and a flat-to-down 2027?

rows.finding: Apple gained 3.9 percentage points of global smartphone share in Q2 2026 to 20.2% on record Q2 shipments (+14.9%) and is on track for a record 22% annual share; iOS reaches 23.6% of 2026 shipments while Apple's own units fall 1.3%; Samsung leads at 22.7% (+3.2pp) and Xiaomi fell 26.4%.
rows.mechanism: Share gains come from supply security and price discipline in a cost shock, not from product innovation: Apple and Samsung held prices while Android peers raised them, so demand migrated up the price ladder.
rows.benchmark: Q1 2026 Samsung 21.2% versus Apple 21.0% (a statistical tie); Q2 2026 Samsung 22.7% versus Apple 20.2%; Xiaomi -26.4% and vivo -19.6% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: The claim that Apple's share gains are structural: they coincide with a one-off memory shock, and IDC expects normalisation only in 2028, after which price-led Android vendors can rebuild.
rows.implication: Underwrite Apple on margin and services rather than on a permanent share gain; the share number to watch is whether iOS holds 22-24% once memory costs normalise in 2028.
rows.confidence: high - IDC final historical data for two consecutive quarters, consistent with Apple's own +22.4% iPhone revenue growth in the first nine months of FY2026
rows.follow_up: What share does iOS hold in 2028 when IDC expects memory supply to normalise?

rows.finding: Apple's nine-month FY2026 segment revenue: Americas $149.4bn (+11.4%), Europe $95.6bn (+16.1%), Greater China $64.8bn (+30.0%), Japan $24.4bn (+10.4%), Rest of Asia Pacific $30.2bn (+19.4%) on total revenue of $364.4bn (+16.2%); Greater China had fallen from $72.6bn in FY2023 to $64.4bn in FY2025 before this rebound.
rows.mechanism: Greater China's swing is the largest single driver of group growth: a $14.9bn increase on a $49.9bn base adds 4.1 percentage points to group growth, and renminbi strength plus iPhone 17 demand did the work; Europe's segment definition includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing geography is inside a line item labelled Europe.
rows.benchmark: FY2023 Greater China $72.6bn, FY2024 $67.0bn, FY2025 $64.4bn (a two-year decline of 11.3%), then +30.0% in the first nine months of FY2026.
rows.weakens: The 2025-era narrative that Apple is losing China permanently; but it also weakens any reading of the regional table as a clean guide to where growth happens, because India is not a separate line.
rows.implication: The revenue mix is shifting toward the faster-growing regions in FY2026, but the swing factor is China, a market where policy and a domestic champion set the terms; an investor should size China at a discount to its 17.8% of revenue.
rows.confidence: high on the figures (audited 10-K plus filed 10-Q), medium on durability of the China rebound
rows.follow_up: How much of the Greater China increase is currency and how much is unit growth, and what happens when the renminbi tailwind reverses?

rows.finding: Services produced $109.2bn (26.2% of FY2025 revenue) at a 75.4% gross margin, grew 14.1% to $91.7bn in the first nine months of FY2026, and is the only large pool where Apple's margin is not capped by hardware competition.
rows.mechanism: Services monetise an installed base that Apple says reached an all-time high in the June 2026 quarter, at near-zero marginal cost, so each incremental dollar of services revenue carries about twice the gross margin of hardware; the adjacent pools are larger than Apple's: Alphabet's trailing-twelve-month revenue is $471.1bn and Netflix's $49.7bn.
rows.benchmark: Products gross margin 36.8% versus Services 75.4% in FY2025; Services grew 14% in FY2025 and 14.1% in the first nine months of FY2026, versus total revenue growth of 6.4% and 16.2%.
rows.weakens: The durability of the take rate: Apple discloses a U.S. court order barring commission on certain external purchases and a DMA compliance plan the European Commission has challenged.
rows.implication: Services is the valuation support, but its growth must be priced net of a lower take rate; the app-economy pool size is not disclosed by any source retrieved, so the section states that gap rather than estimating it.
rows.confidence: high on reported figures, low on the size of the app-economy pool (not disclosed)
rows.follow_up: What share of Services revenue is commission-based and therefore exposed to the U.S. injunction and the DMA?

rows.finding: China is a share fight in a shrinking market: 66m units in Q2 2026 (-4.3%), the fifth consecutive quarterly decline, with Huawei at 22.6% (+19.4%) and Apple at 18.1% (+24.4%); first-half 2026 shipments were 134m units (-4.2%) and IDC expects the decline to widen to about 20% in the second half before a recovery around 2028-2029.
rows.mechanism: Huawei held prices while other Android vendors raised theirs, widened its line-up and leaned on domestic brand loyalty, so it captured the entry and mid tiers; Apple captured the premium tier, which is why Apple's China revenue (+30%) outran its China unit share (18.1%).
rows.benchmark: Huawei 22.6% versus Apple 18.1% in units, but Apple's Greater China revenue per unit is higher: $64.8bn of nine-month revenue against an 18.1% share of a market running at roughly 264m units a year.
rows.weakens: The claim that China revenue follows China unit share; the two diverge by a factor that reflects Apple's price premium, and both can move in opposite directions.
rows.implication: China can grow Apple's revenue while Apple stays second in units, but the Huawei-led price discipline is the mechanism that decides whether that holds; size China exposure with a policy and competition discount.
rows.confidence: high - IDC preliminary quarterly data with vendor-level shares and a stated outlook
rows.follow_up: Does Huawei's HarmonyOS expansion into the entry tier pull first-time buyers away from iOS permanently, or only delay them?

rows.finding: India ships 31.0m smartphones a quarter (-4.1% in Q1 2026) at a record $302 ASP, with the $600-800 band up 32% and Apple fourth by units behind vivo, Samsung and OPPO; the sub-$100 segment fell 59% and its share halved.
rows.mechanism: Memory cost inflation forces Indian buyers up the price ladder faster than incomes rise, which mechanically expands Apple's addressable slice of the market without Apple having to cut price; but the same inflation cuts the number of first-time smartphone buyers who would later upgrade.
rows.benchmark: India ASP $302 versus a global ASP of $581; Apple fourth by units in a market where the $800-plus band is only 7% of shipments.
rows.weakens: The claim that India is Apple's next volume market within the forecast horizon; at a 7% share for the $800-plus band, the near-term revenue contribution is small.
rows.implication: Treat India as a five-year option priced mainly through Services and premium share, not as a driver of FY2027 revenue; the segment table should show it as a planned expansion market inside Europe.
rows.confidence: medium-high - IDC quarterly data for one quarter, with the price-band detail that supports the mechanism
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's unit share and revenue share in India for a full year, and how much of it is manufacturing-linked local content?

plan.decision_question: How large and how fast-growing are the markets Apple serves, and is its revenue mix shifting toward the faster-growing ones?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction — so the market case rests on premiumisation and Services attach rather than device volume, is strongest in the United States and weakest in China, where a domestic champion and a fading subsidy set the terms.
plan.why_different: This section sizes the pools and their growth; it does not explain the product (technology_product), the accounting (financials) or the rivals' strategies as such (competition). It answers whether the demand exists and where, not whether Apple wins it.
plan.mechanism: Memory scarcity raises handset bill-of-materials, entry tiers become unviable, demand migrates up the price ladder, and value concentrates in vendors with supply contracts and premium mix; Apple monetises that migration through a higher ASP and a 75%-gross-margin Services layer on an installed base that keeps growing even when units do not.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own FY2023-FY2025 regional history (Greater China $72.6bn to $64.4bn then +30%), IDC's prior forecast vintages, Samsung and Xiaomi share moves in the same quarters, and Alphabet and Netflix as scale references for the services pool.
plan.counter_evidence: If memory prices normalise in 2028, price-led Android vendors rebuild the entry tier and Apple's share gain reverses; if the App Store take rate is removed by courts and the DMA, Services growth no longer carries the margin mix; and if China's subsidy-driven premium demand fades as it did in Q2 2026, the +30% China line is a one-year currency-and-launch effect rather than a trend.
plan.visual: Two tables: a market-size table (TAM/SAM/SOM with method, publisher and year) and a regional table (Region | market size and year | growth | Apple's position | barriers | key competitors | source).
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong growth, well positioned, clear runway, fierce competition, robust demand, secular tailwind, TAM of $X trillion without a publisher and year, 'about 2.3 billion devices' presented as fact without a source
