rows.finding: Apple's installed base passed 2.5 billion active devices on 2026-01-29, up from more than 2.35 billion a year earlier.
rows.mechanism: A larger installed base raises the monetisable stock behind Services and the future upgrade pool even while annual unit sales fall.
rows.benchmark: The 2.3 billion figure previously used; 2.35 billion a year earlier.
rows.weakens: Apple discloses neither the replacement rate nor the device mix, so the annual upgrade pool cannot be derived from the 2.5 billion stock.
rows.implication: Supports Services attach and premiumisation, and closes the device-count gap, but not the replacement-rate gap that determines annual upgrades.
rows.confidence: high; direct quote from Apple's release, reported the same day
rows.follow_up: What share of the 2.5 billion is active iPhones rather than iPad, Mac, Watch and accessories?

rows.finding: Services was $91.7bn, 25.2% of $364.4bn nine-month FY2026 revenue, up 14%, at a 76.3% gross margin; FY2025 was $109.2bn, 26.2% of revenue.
rows.mechanism: Total revenue grew 16.2%, faster than Services' 14%, so mix shifted toward hardware and China rather than toward the recurring pool.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 Services mix of 26.2%; nine-month FY2025 margin of 75.5%.
rows.weakens: One year's mix can reverse with a launch cycle, and the Services gross margin rose to 76.3%.
rows.implication: The Services-led mix thesis is weaker in FY2026 than the FY2025 snapshot implies; price and China carry growth.
rows.confidence: high; filed figures
rows.follow_up: What share of Services is commission rather than subscription, advertising or licensing?

rows.finding: The Google search-distribution payment was reported at $20bn in 2022, equal to 17% of trailing Services revenue of $120.5bn and 22% of trailing Services gross profit of $91.6bn.
rows.mechanism: One licensing payment concentrated in Services ties Apple's highest-margin revenue to a single counterparty's antitrust exposure.
rows.benchmark: The valuation work capitalises it at about $450bn at 30x, near 9% of market value; that is a multiple-based estimate, not a disclosed value.
rows.weakens: The numerator is a 2022 figure, Apple does not disclose the current amount, and the ratios mix a 2022 numerator with 2026 denominators.
rows.implication: Price the payment as a live policy risk, but not as a loss already incurred.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What is the current annual payment and its renewal terms?

rows.finding: No default-payment ban is in force: the 2025-09-02 remedies decision declined to ban distributor payments, the December 2025 final judgment restricting distribution is under appeal by Google (2026-01) and the DOJ (2026-02), pending at 2026-10-29.
rows.mechanism: Remedies litigation runs slower than headline risk; the revenue remains until a final, non-appealed order.
rows.benchmark: The secondary claim of an April 2026 order and June 2026 ban (S165) against the court record summarised in S118 and Alphabet's 10-Q (S42).
rows.weakens: S165 asserts a ban that a material fact in Alphabet's October 2026 filing would have disclosed; the claim is unsupported and not used.
rows.implication: Do not price an immediate loss; price the appeal outcome and the 2027-2028 timing.
rows.confidence: high that the ban claim is unsupported; medium on the ultimate outcome
rows.follow_up: What does the final judgment say about default payments, and when will the D.C. Circuit rule?

rows.finding: Worldwide smartphone shipments fall 16.7% to just over 1.0bn units in 2026 while value rises 6.3% to $613bn and ASP reaches $581, up 27.6%.
rows.mechanism: Memory costs remove the entry tier and lift ASP; unit-share gains bought with early memory supply flatter Apple through 2027.
rows.benchmark: IDC's prior $550 ASP; bottom-up 1.0bn units x $581 = $581bn, within 5% of $613bn.
rows.weakens: The figures are third-party estimates, and a 2028 entry-tier recovery could reverse Apple's share gain.
rows.implication: Revenue growth must come from price and mix, not volume; 2028 is the test when memory normalises.
rows.confidence: high for 2026; medium for 2027-2028
rows.follow_up: When does IDC expect memory prices to normalise, and what unit recovery follows?

rows.finding: Greater China revenue was $64.8bn in nine months of FY2026, up 30.0% on $49.9bn, while Apple held 18.1% of Q2 2026 units behind Huawei's 22.6%.
rows.mechanism: China growth is a price, currency and launch effect while unit share remains second, so the mix shifts toward the most politically exposed region.
rows.benchmark: Greater China revenue of $72.6bn in FY2023 and $64.4bn in FY2025; Americas grew 11.4%.
rows.weakens: Renminbi strength and pull-forward ahead of second-half price increases; IDC sees China down as much as 20% in H2 2026.
rows.implication: China durability is the swing factor for the FY2026 growth rate and for the premiumisation case beyond 2027.
rows.confidence: high on the figures; medium on durability
rows.follow_up: How much of the 30% increase is currency, and what was the June-quarter unit trend?

rows.finding: Apple leads no hardware category outright except detachable tablets: it is second in global smartphones (20.2% in Q2 2026 behind Samsung's 22.7%), second in PCs and tablets combined (18.2% behind Lenovo's 20.1%), holds 55.3% of detachables, is first in total wearables (15.5%) but second in smartwatches (17.2% to Huawei's 18.8%).
rows.mechanism: Apple wins where tight hardware-software integration is the buyer's deciding attribute (detachables, earwear) and loses where scale and price set the market (smartphones, notebooks, smartwatches), so its economics depend on holding a premium price on a minority unit share rather than on converting the market.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own 10-K states it has a minority share in global smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables; Samsung at 22.7%, Lenovo at 20.1%, Huawei at 18.8% of smartwatches.
rows.weakens: Any framing of Apple as the market leader in phones or PCs; the 10-K's own language contradicts it.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite an Apple share story; underwrite a margin story. The premium position is a price position, and price positions erode when a lower-cost rival reaches parity on the features buyers check.
rows.confidence: high - IDC quarterly tracker data for a single quarter plus Apple's primary filing
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's value share, as opposed to unit share, in each category, and is there a published revenue-share series?

rows.finding: Samsung grew shipments 8.1% and gained 3.2 percentage points in Q2 2026 while every Chinese Android vendor in the top five fell by double digits; IDC attributes the split to secured memory supply, and Apple's 1.3% unit decline in 2026 against Android's 24.3% comes from the same mechanism.
rows.mechanism: In a component shortage the binding constraint is supply access, not product design: a vendor that makes its own memory can hold handset prices and take share while rivals pass cost through, so Samsung profits on both sides of Apple's bill of materials.
rows.benchmark: Xiaomi fell 26.4% and vivo 19.6% in the same quarter; the sub-$100 segment fell almost 60% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: The reading that Apple's 2026 share gain is a verdict on product quality, and the assumption that Apple's supply chain is a durable moat rather than a one-year sourcing feat.
rows.implication: Samsung is the most dangerous competitor, and the threat is vertical integration in memory rather than a better phone; that is a cost-of-goods threat Apple can only answer with long-term supply contracts and price, which is exactly what it did in 2026.
rows.confidence: high on the share data, medium on the attribution cause
rows.follow_up: How much of Samsung's handset cost advantage comes from internal memory supply, and would a Korean won or memory-price reversal remove it?

rows.finding: Apple enters foldables in the second half of 2026 and IDC expects it to ship more than 17m foldable iPhones by 2027, about 40% of a category growing 12.6% in 2026 to 22.9m units and 18% in 2027, at an ASP above $2,550 generating over $45.7bn of value, more than half the category.
rows.mechanism: A late entrant with a much higher price can still capture the category's value if its brand carries the premium: Apple converts a declining niche into the only growing smartphone segment, which raises blended ASP without needing volume.
rows.benchmark: Apple's foldable ASP above $2,550 against a global smartphone ASP of $581; category size 22.9m units in 2026 against a market of about 1bn.
rows.weakens: The claim that Apple's innovation cycle has stalled; but it also caps the upside, because 22.9m units is roughly 2% of the smartphone market.
rows.implication: Foldables support the average-selling-price and margin line rather than unit growth, and they open a direct challenge to Samsung and Huawei in the one premium segment those two had held alone.
rows.confidence: medium - a forecast from a single agency, with Apple's own product not yet through a full cycle
rows.follow_up: What is the gross margin on the foldable, and does the hinge and display supply chain give Apple a cost advantage or a cost penalty?

rows.finding: The App Store's commission is being removed by courts and regulators rather than by a competing store: Apple's FY2025 10-K discloses that it is subject to a U.S. court order preventing it from imposing any commission on certain external purchases, that its DMA compliance plan has been challenged by the European Commission, and that it faces U.S. monopolization suits over smartphones.
rows.mechanism: A regulated platform loses pricing power at the point of payment: if developers can route buyers to the web, Apple's commission falls toward a payment-processing fee, and the profit pool that funds the premium hardware position shrinks without any rival winning a single device sale.
rows.benchmark: Epic Games' litigation against the App Store; the European Commission's DMA enforcement against Apple's compliance plan; Google's own search-distribution remedies order of 2025-09-02.
rows.weakens: The claim that Apple's ecosystem lock-in protects Services pricing indefinitely, and any valuation that capitalises the 2026 Services margin as permanent.
rows.implication: Services growth should be valued at a lower multiple than its 14% growth and 75% gross margin imply, and the take rate, not store share, is the metric to underwrite.
rows.confidence: high on the legal facts, low on the revenue at risk (not disclosed)
rows.follow_up: What proportion of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription or advertising, and what take rate survives in the United States and the EU in 2027?

rows.finding: AI is the one product dimension where Apple is not ahead: Samsung shipped the Galaxy S26 Ultra with AI features that IDC credits for its return to first place in Q1 2026, Huawei scales a domestic operating system to 51m units, and Apple's answer, the all-new Siri AI, arrived at WWDC26 with research and development spending up 32.5% to $34.0bn in the first nine months of FY2026.
rows.mechanism: When a feature becomes the reason a buyer upgrades, the vendor that ships it first sets the comparison; Apple's late launch means it competes on integration and privacy rather than on capability, which protects loyalty but not price.
rows.benchmark: Huawei's HarmonyOS at 51m units in 2026 against 22.6% China share, and Apple's own Siri AI launched at WWDC26 in June 2026.
rows.weakens: The assumption that Apple's integration advantage converts into an AI advantage; IDC's China commentary names AI competition as a factor in the premium tier.
rows.implication: Watch AI-driven share loss in China in 2027 as the leading indicator; if it appears, the premium price that funds the model is exposed before unit share moves.
rows.confidence: medium - direction supported, but no measured share effect of AI features on purchases in the sources retrieved
rows.follow_up: Do AI features change purchase intent in China and the United States, and does Apple's Siri AI run on-device or through a partner model, with what cost per query?

rows.finding: The largest competitor is the phone already in the buyer's hand: replacement cycles are lengthening, entry-level buyers are leaving the market rather than trading up, and IDC expects demand to return only when a replacement cycle comes due in 2028-2029.
rows.mechanism: A working device is a substitute for a new one at any price above zero, so the elasticity of upgrade timing, not the features of a rival phone, sets the volume; Apple's installed base grows slowly while its revenue per device rises.
rows.benchmark: China's 66m units a quarter, of which Apple takes 18.1%; 173m sub-$100 units shipped globally in 2025 now becoming unviable; IDC's statement that consumers are postponing rather than abandoning upgrades.
rows.weakens: Forecasts that treat a 2026 share gain as a demand inflection; IDC's China note explicitly describes demand as deferred, not destroyed, and Apple's rise as partly pull-forward.
rows.implication: Longer cycles support Services revenue and suppress hardware units, which is consistent with Apple's reported mix; but it also means the FY2026 iPhone growth rate is not a base for FY2027.
rows.confidence: high - three independent IDC datasets agree on the direction
rows.follow_up: What is the measured average replacement cycle now, and how much of Apple's FY2026 iPhone growth is pull-forward ahead of expected price increases rather than new demand?

plan.decision_question: Is Apple's competitive position strengthening or eroding, product by product and region by region?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's competitive position strengthened in 2026 in every hardware line except smartwatches, but the strengthening is crisis-specific — bought with memory supply and price discipline rather than product superiority — and it is being offset where it matters most for profit, because the App Store commission that funds the premium position is being dismantled by courts and the DMA rather than by a rival's product.
plan.why_different: This section identifies who takes the buyer and the profit pool, product by product and region by region; the market section sizes the pool and the financial section explains the accounting. Only here are rivals' shares, prices and legal constraints compared directly with Apple's.
plan.mechanism: Apple's 2026 gains come from secured memory supply, price discipline and premium mix rather than from product superiority, so the advantage is strongest where buyers can finance an $800-plus device and weakest where a domestic champion prices in local currency under a domestic operating system; meanwhile the profit pool that funds the position, the App Store commission, is being removed by courts and the DMA rather than by a competitor's product.
plan.comparison_set: Samsung (22.7% global units, 8.1% growth), Xiaomi (-26.4%), Huawei (22.6% in China, +19.9%), Lenovo (20.1% of PCs), HP and Dell, and for Services Alphabet (trailing-twelve-month revenue $471.1bn) and Netflix ($49.7bn) as scale references, against Apple's own 10-K admission of minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables.
plan.counter_evidence: Huawei's 22.6% China share with a domestic operating system; a U.S. court order that already bars Apple from charging commission on certain external purchases; a DMA compliance plan the European Commission has challenged; and the fact that Apple's own 10-K concedes minority share in every hardware category, so the premium position is a margin position, not a unit market position.
plan.visual: Per-product competitor table with share, technology, price position and source; plus a positioning table (product by leader, challenger, niche, emerging threat) and a SWOT component.
plan.prohibited: fierce competition, strong moat, well positioned, clearly winning, best-in-class, 'Apple dominates' without a product and a share figure, unqualified '2.3 billion installed base'

rows.finding: FY2025 net income rose 19.5% to $112,010M, but pretax income rose only 7.5% ($132,729M vs $123,485M) while the tax provision fell 30.3% to $20,719M from $29,749M; FY2024 carried the one-time $10.2bn Irish State Aid charge (a $15.8bn payment to Ireland less a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit and $823M of released unrecognised benefits). Normalising FY2024 at FY2025's 15.6% effective rate gives $104,222M, so underlying net income growth was 7.5%.
rows.mechanism: A one-off tax charge in the base year, not a change in trading, produced half of the following year's net income growth - the classic base-effect distortion in a two-year comparison.
rows.benchmark: Reported FY2025 net income growth of +19.5% and diluted EPS growth of +22.7% ($6.08 to $7.46).
rows.weakens: The reading that Apple's FY2025 was an acceleration year; on a normalised tax rate the company grew earnings at roughly the rate of revenue.
rows.implication: Halve the growth rate you extrapolate. The 22.7% EPS growth of FY2025 is a tax-base artefact as much as an operating result, and the FY2026 comparison is against a clean base, so any FY2026 deceleration is not a deterioration.
rows.confidence: high - both the provision and the charge are audited and disclosed
rows.follow_up: What is the sustainable effective tax rate under OECD Pillar Two, and how much of the $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits (up to $6bn of which may move within 12 months) is a cash exposure?

rows.finding: Buybacks contributed about 5.4 points of the 21.7% EPS growth from FY2023 to FY2025, so roughly a quarter of EPS growth was a smaller denominator; in the trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 the contribution fell to about 1.9 points (EPS +16.9%, net income +15.1%) because repurchases slowed to $62,094M in the nine months from $70,579M a year earlier while free cash flow rose 43% to $116,996M from $81,754M.
rows.mechanism: At a constant net income, a 5% smaller share count adds 5% to EPS with no operating improvement; the mechanism reverses when the repurchase pace slows, which is what happened in FY2026.
rows.benchmark: FY2023-FY2025: net income +15.5%, diluted EPS +21.7%, diluted shares -5.1% (15,813M to 15,005M), on $258,212M of cumulative buybacks.
rows.weakens: The view that Apple's EPS growth is understated by buybacks and that management will keep shrinking the count at the same rate.
rows.implication: The buyback is a real but shrinking contributor; do not model EPS growth the way FY2023-FY2025 delivered it, because the pace of repurchase has already slowed and net cash is building instead.
rows.confidence: high - share counts and repurchase cash flows are disclosed
rows.follow_up: Why did Apple cut the repurchase pace by 12% while free cash flow rose 43%, building $28bn of net cash - is it tariff or AI investment, or price discipline at 39.5x earnings?

rows.finding: Cash paid for income taxes was $43,369M in FY2025, or 32.7% of pretax income, against a $20,719M tax provision and a 15.6% book rate - the widest gap in the three years - and free cash flow fell to 0.88x of net income from 1.16x, despite operating cash flow of $111,482M; by the trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27 the ratio had recovered to 1.06x on $146,724M of operating cash flow and $10,041M of capex.
rows.mechanism: Deferred and settlement payments decouple cash tax from book tax; when the cash rate exceeds the book rate the accounting profit overstates distributable cash for that period, and free cash flow per share - not EPS - is the better measure of what funds the buyback.
rows.benchmark: FY2024 FCF/net income of 1.16x and FY2023 of 1.03x; FY2023 cash taxes were 16.4% of pretax income and FY2024 were 21.1%.
rows.weakens: Simple FCF-to-net-income ratios and any valuation that capitalises net income without checking the cash tax line.
rows.implication: The 15.6% book tax rate is not the cash tax rate; on FY2025 evidence, a third of pretax income left as cash tax, which matters for anyone valuing Apple on net income rather than on cash.
rows.confidence: high on the figures; medium on the driver, because Apple does not reconcile the cash tax figure to the Irish settlement line by line
rows.follow_up: Which payments drove the $43.4bn of FY2025 cash taxes, and does the FY2026 profile normalise once the final $8.8bn of TCJA repatriation tax was paid in the nine months to 2026-06-27?

rows.finding: Inventory rose to $11,092M at 2026-06-27 from $5,925M a year earlier, an 87% increase against 16.2% revenue growth, lifting days inventory to 16.9 from 9.4 and pulling the cash conversion cycle to -56.8 days from -71.1; receivables fell to $31,398M from $39,777M at the FY2025 year-end and payables to $64,525M from $69,860M.
rows.mechanism: Negative working capital is a funding source only while payables and deferred revenue grow faster than inventory and receivables; when inventory nearly doubles, the supplier-funded float shrinks and the cash goes into stock.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 days inventory of 9.4 and cash conversion cycle of -71.1 days at the September year-end; Q3 FY2025 inventory of $5,925M at the same seasonal point.
rows.weakens: The claim that Apple's negative working capital is a permanent, stable source of cash.
rows.implication: Ask for the inventory composition before accepting the 50.1% gross margin: a build of this size either finances a strong December quarter or precedes a write-down, and the answer is not in the filings yet.
rows.confidence: high on the balance-sheet change; medium on the cause, which Apple describes only as component cost and supply pressure
rows.follow_up: Is the $5.2bn inventory build pre-tariff and pre-launch stock, or unsold units - and what does the FY2026 10-K show about inventory valuation and any write-down?

rows.finding: At 2026-06-27 Apple held $39,544M of cash plus $106,973M of marketable securities against $84,344M of debt, for net cash of $62,173M, up from $33,763M nine months earlier; commercial paper fell to $1,997M from $7,979M, and off-balance-sheet commitments included $57.0bn of manufacturing purchase obligations ($56.2bn due within twelve months) and $29.3bn of other purchase obligations.
rows.mechanism: Apple funds itself from operations and holds more securities than debt, so the interest line nets to near zero; the meaningful financial commitment is the forward purchase book that fixes component supply and, with it, the cost base.
rows.benchmark: Net cash of $33,763M at 2025-09-27, total debt of $98,657M, and interest expense not separately tagged because other income absorbs it (net other expense of $321M in FY2025).
rows.weakens: Any concern framed as leverage or interest cover; equally, it weakens the use of net cash as a valuation add-on, since most of it is working capital and tax reserve rather than surplus.
rows.implication: Balance-sheet risk is not the issue - refinancing, interest cover and liquidity are all comfortable; the real commitment is the $57bn purchase obligation, which is a cost risk rather than a solvency risk.
rows.confidence: high - all balances are on the face of the statements
rows.follow_up: How much of the $57.0bn manufacturing commitment is priced on memory and NAND at current spot, and what happens to the gross margin if those prices stay elevated for four quarters?

rows.finding: Apple's trailing-twelve-month return on equity was 148.8% and return on invested capital 320.6% on invested capital of about $45,347M (equity of $107,520M plus debt of $84,344M less $146,517M of cash and securities), against a return on assets of 36.1% and an operating margin of 33.2%.
rows.mechanism: Buybacks and large cash balances shrink invested capital, so ROIC mechanically rises with financial policy rather than operating performance; ROE is distorted the same way when equity is $107,520M on $128,930M of net income.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft FY2026 ROIC 35.9% and Alphabet FY2025 ROIC 37.0%, both computed on invested capital in the hundreds of billions.
rows.weakens: Cross-company ROIC comparisons that put Apple's triple-digit figure beside Microsoft's 35.9% as if the denominators were alike.
rows.implication: Do not read 320% ROIC as a quality score; the denominator has been shrunk by $258bn of buybacks and by holding cash. ROA of 36.1% is the honest number, and it is still the best in the peer set.
rows.confidence: high on the figures; the comparison is limited by how differently the four companies are capitalised
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's return on gross capital employed including the supplier and contract-manufacturing assets it does not own, and is that the right denominator to compare with Microsoft's 35.9%?

rows.finding: Greater China revenue rose 30% to $64,839M in the nine months to 2026-06-27 and 22% to $18,816M in the June quarter, so nine months already exceed the whole of FY2025's $64,377M after two years of decline; on sensitivity, three points of gross margin on TTM revenue of $466,823M is $14,005M of pretax profit, or 9.0% of TTM net income, and losing the $20bn search payment at near-100% incremental margin would remove about $16,540M after tax, or 12.8%.
rows.mechanism: Gross margin and a single licensing line are both high-margin and both politically or cyclically exposed, so they dominate the variance; revenue growth at a 49% margin matters less per point than a margin change at constant revenue.
rows.benchmark: Greater China revenue of $72,559M in FY2023, $66,952M in FY2024 (-8%) and $64,377M in FY2025 (-4%); TTM net income of $128,930M and TTM EPS of $8.72.
rows.weakens: The bear case built mainly on China share loss - on the latest three quarters, Greater China is the fastest-growing large segment, not the weakest.
rows.implication: The two variables that move the outcome most are gross margin and the search payment, not revenue growth - a 3-point margin give-back and the loss of the search deal together would cut TTM net income by about 22%.
rows.confidence: high on the segment and sensitivity arithmetic; medium on the Google amount, which is a 2022 court figure
rows.follow_up: Is the Greater China rebound volume or price, and how much of it is the iPhone 17 cycle rather than a durable share recovery against Huawei?

plan.decision_question: Are Apple's earnings and cash flow as high-quality as the multiple implies, and what would break the quality?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's cash conversion and balance sheet are as good as the multiple implies, but the earnings growth is not: FY2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes roughly 10% once the $10.2bn Irish tax charge in the prior year is normalised out, and FY2026's margin is being flattered by a tariff refund Apple does not quantify.
plan.why_different: This section tests the statements and their notes for quality - what the tax line, the buyback, working capital and the non-cash items do to reported growth; the business model section explains where the revenue comes from, and the valuation section decides what multiple to pay for it.
plan.mechanism: Buybacks shrink the share count against a rising net income, so EPS outgrows net income; the tax line, not operations, drove half of FY2025's net income growth after the Irish charge; and negative working capital plus a capital-light model let Apple convert net income into free cash at close to 1x, which peers spending a third of revenue on capex cannot.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own FY2023-FY2025 and TTM record; Microsoft FY2026, Alphabet FY2025 and Meta FY2025 on margin, capex intensity, cash conversion, ROIC and stock-based compensation; the 10-year Treasury yield of 4.93% as the cost of the buyback.
plan.counter_evidence: FY2025's 22.7% EPS growth is roughly half tax-base effect from the $10.2bn Irish State Aid charge in FY2024; cash taxes paid were $43,369M against a $20,719M provision; inventory rose 87% year on year to $11,092M; the FY2026 gross margin carries an unquantified tariff refund; and $20bn of search licensing sits with one counterparty under appeal.
plan.visual: A three-year plus TTM statement table and a returns and working-capital table, with a warning box on the tariff refund, the inventory build and the cash-versus-book tax gap.
plan.prohibited: banned_empty_phrases: 'fortress balance sheet', 'high-quality earnings' without definition, 'risks are manageable', 'well positioned', 'strong cash generation'; banned_patterns: quoting EPS growth without the tax normalisation in the same sentence, quoting ROE or ROIC without noting the buyback and net-cash distortion, any full-year FY2026 figure that the filings do not contain.

rows.finding: The European Commission fined Apple €500m on 2025-04-23 for breaching the DMA anti-steering obligation and issued a cease and desist order; the parallel Article 6(4) investigation into alternative-app terms remains open with a statutory ceiling of 10% of annual worldwide net sales, and Apple has appealed the Article 5(4) decision.
rows.mechanism: A regulator sets the price of the App Store toll in its jurisdiction and can escalate to a revenue-based fine, so the compliance cost is a recurring operating expense rather than a one-off legal charge.
rows.benchmark: Meta was fined €200m in the same 2025-04-23 package; Google was fined €890m on 2026-07-23 for Play steering and search self-preferencing; Alphabet's Android case produced a €4.1bn fine affirmed in 2022 and finally upheld by the ECJ in July 2026.
rows.weakens: The Commission closed its separate Apple user-choice investigation on the same day and found on 2026-02-05 that Apple Ads and Apple Maps should not be designated, so the DMA's reach over Apple is narrower than headlines imply; no further Apple DMA fine appears through 2026-09-28.
rows.implication: Price the DMA as a permanent 100-200bp drag on EU App Store take rate plus a tail fine, not as a solvency event.
rows.confidence: high - primary regulator release plus two Apple filings
rows.follow_up: Does the Article 6(4) file end in a second fine before the 2027 appeal ruling, and what fee structure does Apple's EU compliance plan now carry?

rows.finding: The N.D. Cal. found Apple in civil contempt on 2025-04-30 and barred any commission on out-of-app purchases; the Ninth Circuit modified that on 2025-12-11 to allow parity requirements and some commission on link-outs, and the Supreme Court granted cert on 2026-06-30 limited to the civil-contempt standard.
rows.mechanism: Judicial remedies reset the US App Store commission on digital goods bought through external links, the highest-margin revenue line Apple has; a contempt finding also shifts the default in later disputes toward stricter remedies.
rows.benchmark: Apple's US storefront historically charged 15-30% on in-app digital purchases; the 2025 injunction took that to zero on out-of-app purchases before the Ninth Circuit reinstated a partial fee.
rows.weakens: The Ninth Circuit expressly held Apple can charge some commission and the Supreme Court review is about the contempt standard, not the injunction's antitrust merits, so a total loss of US commission is not the base case.
rows.implication: Assume a permanent step-down in US link-out commission; this is the single most concrete Services gross-profit leak in the file.
rows.confidence: high - company disclosure of court orders, dated to the day
rows.follow_up: What fee has Apple actually set on US link-out purchases since the December 2025 remand, and what share of US digital-goods spend has moved off in-app purchase?

rows.finding: The Google search remedies decision of 2025-09-02 rejected Chrome and Android divestiture, barred exclusive distribution deals for six years but expressly permitted Google to keep paying distributors such as Apple for default placement if the deals are non-exclusive and run one year or less; a final judgment was entered in December 2025 and both sides' appeals were pending at 2026-10-29.
rows.mechanism: The court protected the payment stream to avoid harming device makers, so Apple's search-distribution revenue survives but loses its exclusivity and multi-year lock-in, which transfers pricing power to Apple at each annual renewal.
rows.benchmark: The plaintiffs sought a near-total ban on search-related payments to distribution partners; the court rejected it, citing the harm to device makers, carriers and browser developers.
rows.weakens: Apple does not disclose the payment; the roughly $20bn-a-year figure used in press coverage is unverified in Apple's filings, and a one-year term cap plus mandatory choice screens could erode it at the next renewal.
rows.implication: Treat the search payment as intact through 2027 with renegotiation risk each year, not as an expiring asset.
rows.confidence: high on the legal terms, low on the dollar amount
rows.follow_up: What does Apple's next Safari default agreement look like after the one-year term cap, and has Apple begun surfacing alternative search or AI assistants?

rows.finding: US tariff exposure was re-priced twice in 2026: the Section 232 semiconductor investigation's initial results on 2026-01-14 imposed no additional tariff on Apple products, and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, with Apple claiming refunds recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales; Section 301 tariffs were then imposed.
rows.mechanism: Tariffs hit products gross margin directly and are only partly offset by shifting assembly to India and Vietnam, so the risk is a margin level shift rather than a demand shock.
rows.benchmark: Section 232 semiconductor tariffs were widely expected to capture downstream devices containing chips; the initial results spared them, against a base case of a mid-single-digit percentage tariff on China-assembled iPhones.
rows.weakens: Apple warns that further Section 232 or Section 301 measures remain possible and that rare-earth and component availability could still bite; the truce that underpins the calm expires 2027-01-10.
rows.implication: Remove the 2025-style tariff cliff from the near-term model but keep a standing margin haircut for Section 301 and future sector actions.
rows.confidence: high - company disclosure in the Q3 FY2026 10-Q
rows.follow_up: What net tariff cost is embedded in the FY2027 products gross-margin guide, and how much China assembly remains for US-bound units?

rows.finding: The opposite of the China-closure case happened: China's CAC registered Apple Intelligence for the mainland market on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu, and Greater China net sales rose to $18,816m in Q3 FY2026 from $15,369m a year earlier, up 22%, and to $64,839m for the nine months from $49,884m, up 30%.
rows.mechanism: Data and AI rules act as a market-access gate: once a foreign model is registered with a domestic partner, the gate becomes a toll and a localisation requirement rather than a prohibition.
rows.benchmark: Apple Intelligence had been unavailable in China since its 2024 debut, a 21-22 month gap that fed the share-loss narrative to Huawei.
rows.weakens: Registration is not the same as launch at scale, and the truce that covers rare-earth and tariff escalation expires 2027-01-10, so a political reversal would re-open the gate.
rows.implication: The China regulatory tail is smaller than the bear case assumes; the demand question is competitive, not regulatory.
rows.confidence: medium - secondary reporting on the CAC registration, primary on the revenue
rows.follow_up: Has Apple Intelligence shipped to mainstream Chinese users, and what data-localisation obligations attach to the Alibaba and Baidu arrangements?

rows.finding: The Irish state-aid case closed against Apple: the ECJ set aside the General Court on 2024-09-10 and confirmed the 2016 decision, producing a $10.2bn net one-time tax charge and $15.8bn payable to Ireland in Q4 FY2024; the FY2025 effective tax rate was 15.6% against 24.1% in FY2024, with $23.2bn of gross unrecognised tax benefits outstanding.
rows.mechanism: Tax is a jurisdiction-allocation negotiation: the one-off is sunk, but the structural risk is that Pillar Two's 15% floor and EU state-aid precedent remove the gap between Apple's foreign rate and the US rate.
rows.benchmark: A 15.6% FY2025 effective rate sits just above the OECD Pillar Two 15% minimum, leaving little room for further erosion but also little incremental Pillar Two cost.
rows.weakens: Apple's 10-K does not quantify a Pillar Two charge and the $23.2bn of unrecognised benefits ($10.6bn rate-relevant) is a two-way risk that could swing the rate either way.
rows.implication: Treat tax as a settled cost, not a lever; do not underwrite future EPS growth from a lower tax rate.
rows.confidence: high on the historical figures, medium on forward Pillar Two exposure
rows.follow_up: What Pillar Two top-up tax did Apple accrue in FY2026, and how much of the $23.2bn of unrecognised benefits relates to transfer pricing rather than the Irish case?

rows.finding: Supply-chain ESG is Apple's strongest record in this file: 100% of identified 3TG smelters and refiners in its supply chain participated in independent third-party conflict-minerals audits for the tenth consecutive year at 2024-12-31, no smelter was found to have financed armed groups, and in June 2024 Apple told suppliers to stop sourcing 3TG from DRC and Rwanda.
rows.mechanism: Audited downstream traceability converts a reputational tail into a procurement cost, which is why Apple can keep selling into regulated Western markets without a forced-labour delisting event.
rows.benchmark: The 3TG audit standard (OECD due diligence, independent third-party audit) is the base rate for large hardware OEMs; ten consecutive years at 100% is at the top of the range.
rows.weakens: The report covers minerals, not assembly labour or Uyghur forced-labour allegations in components, and it is the company's own filing with no independent verification of the underlying audits.
rows.implication: No ESG discount on sourcing; the residual risk is assembly labour in China and India, which these audits do not cover.
rows.confidence: medium-high - primary filing, company-prepared audit summary
rows.follow_up: What third-party audit evidence covers assembly labour in China and India, and has any supplier been terminated over labour findings in the past three years?

rows.finding: Governance is clean on control but not on compliance conduct: Apple has a single class of common stock, an independent Chair separated from the CEO, an Audit Committee that met nine times in 2025 and oversees privacy, cybersecurity, tax and enterprise risk, and related-party disclosures limited to one family-member employment; yet a federal court found it in civil contempt in April 2025 and referred it to the U.S. Attorney for a criminal-contempt determination.
rows.mechanism: A one-share-one-vote board aligned with shareholders reduces extraction risk; a contempt finding shows management chose litigation over compliance in a core profit pool, which raises the probability of stricter remedies in the next case.
rows.benchmark: Peers: Alphabet and Meta both operate dual-class structures; Apple does not, so control risk is lower even though its enforcement record is worse.
rows.weakens: The contempt finding is on appeal and the Supreme Court took the case on the legal standard, so it may not survive as a finding of wrongdoing.
rows.implication: Governance is an asset; compliance culture is the liability. Price a higher probability of adverse remedies, not a discount for control.
rows.confidence: high - proxy and 10-K disclosure
rows.follow_up: Did the U.S. Attorney decline or open a criminal-contempt inquiry, and how has Apple changed its App Review compliance function since April 2025?

plan.decision_question: Which policy, legal and ESG exposures can impair Apple's cash flow, margin or licence to operate, and how much of that is already priced?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's policy exposure is not a licence-to-operate threat but a slow, legislated tax on Services gross profit: the €500m DMA fine and the 2025 US contempt finding show a company that litigates rather than complies, while the three remedies that actually matter - Google's default payment, the US link-out commission and the EU fee structure - have so far been reshaped rather than removed.
plan.why_different: The other sections price demand, mix and multiples; this one prices the legal and policy claim on a slice of Services gross profit and the compliance-culture discount that belongs in the required return, not in the revenue line.
plan.mechanism: Remedies move pricing power from Apple's App Store toll to developers and consumers; each basis point of Services gross margin is worth roughly a tenth of a billion dollars on Apple's scale, so a 100-200bp take-rate cut is an earnings event, not an existential one. Compliance-culture findings raise the probability of stricter remedies next time.
plan.comparison_set: DMA and antitrust enforcement against Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Samsung: Meta €200m (2025-04-23), Google €890m (2026-07-23), Alphabet Android €4.1bn affirmed 2022 and finally upheld July 2026, Amazon and Microsoft cloud designation proceedings opened 2026-06-25; Samsung has no DMA gatekeeper designation. Base rate: fines are frequent, structural break-ups are not.
plan.counter_evidence: Greater China net sales up 30% for the nine months to 2026-06-27 and CAC registration of Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 undercut the China-closure case; the Ninth Circuit restored a commission on link-outs; the Commission closed the user-choice probe and declined to designate Apple Ads and Maps; Section 232 initial results imposed no tariff; no further Apple DMA fine appears through 2026-09-28.
plan.visual: Policy impact matrix (Factor | Exposure | Probability | Impact | Mitigant | Source) plus the regulatory record table
plan.prohibited: risks are manageable; well positioned; high barriers to entry; huge market; fierce competition; about/roughly counts without a source; any sentence about how the section is written

rows.finding: Apple closed at $344.63 on NasdaqGS on 2026-10-30, market capitalisation $5,029.6B and enterprise value $4,967.4B, at 39.5x trailing EPS of $8.72, 35.2x forward EPS (implied $9.79) and EV/EBIT 32.1x; the peer median is 21.0x P/E and 21.2x EV/EBIT, and the S&P 500 is 21.76x trailing and 18.40x forward.
rows.mechanism: The multiple is the price of duration: at 39.5x the earnings yield is 2.53% against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the holder accepts less current yield than the risk-free asset and is paid only if earnings compound; the same price is an 88% premium to the software mega-cap median.
rows.benchmark: MSFT 27.3x, GOOGL 14.6x, META 21.0x (median 21.0x), Samsung 12.5x; S&P 500 18.40x forward / 21.76x trailing; Apple's own 10-year mean 25.35x.
rows.weakens: Apple's 2.7% FCF yield is the highest of the four mega-caps and its P/FCF of 36.8x is a 43% discount to the peer median of 64.6x, because capex is $10.0B against hyperscaler AI budgets; on cash flow Apple is the cheapest of the group, not the dearest.
rows.implication: Do not buy at $344.63 on value grounds: any return must come from earnings growth or a further re-rating, so the section's answer is a price band, not a purchase.
rows.confidence: high — last close, TTM EPS and peer multiples all dated 2026-10-30 and built from SEC XBRL and Yahoo prices.
rows.follow_up: Does the 2026-11-02 Q4 release show a clean 50% gross margin without the tariff refund, and does forward EPS hold above $9.79?

rows.finding: A ten-year reverse DCF on enterprise value of $4,967.4B, TTM free cash flow of $136.7B, 3.0% terminal growth and an 8.5% WACC implies 11.8% annual FCF growth for ten years; the implied growth is 10.5% at an 8.0% WACC and 13.4% at 9.0%. Apple's FCF grew from $93.0B in FY2021 to $98.8B in FY2025, a 1.5% compound rate.
rows.mechanism: The terminal value is capitalised at 18.7x FCF against today's 36.3x EV/FCF, so the model already assumes the multiple halves by 2036 and still needs double-digit FCF growth to justify today's price; the growth has to come from the business, not from re-rating.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own FY2021-FY2025 FCF CAGR of 1.5% and revenue CAGR of 3.3%; IDC's device pools compound at about 1.5% a year to 2030, so 11.8% must come from price, Services and mix.
rows.weakens: TTM FCF of $136.7B is a working-capital and margin high against FY2025's $98.8B; on the lower base the same enterprise value implies about 16% growth, so the result is sensitive to which FCF base is normal.
rows.implication: No margin of safety at $344.63; at a 6% FCF growth path the same DCF gives about $221 a share, at 8% about $255 and at 10% about $298.
rows.confidence: medium-high — the arithmetic is reproducible, but the FCF base and the 65/35 opex assumptions are analyst judgements.
rows.follow_up: What normalised FCF does the FY2026 10-K support once inventory and the tariff refund are stripped out?

rows.finding: Sum of the parts: products revenue $346.3B and gross profit $135.5B, Services revenue $120.5B and gross profit $91.6B on trailing twelve months; at 3-5x EV/Sales for products and 10-14x for Services the parts are worth $2.25-3.42T, against an enterprise value of $4.97T. To reach $4.97T with products at 5x sales, Services must be capitalised at about 27x revenue.
rows.mechanism: The market is paying for the ecosystem and the buyback as a single cash-flow stream, not for what hardware and services would fetch as separate peer-valued businesses; the premium is 31-55% above the parts.
rows.benchmark: MSFT 11.1x EV/Sales, GOOGL 7.1x, META 6.6x, Samsung 12.5x P/E for hardware.
rows.weakens: Apple does not report segment operating income, so the 65/35 opex split is an assumption; Apple's 39.1% product gross margin is far above Samsung or PC hardware peers, so a pure peer multiple understates the hardware franchise.
rows.implication: The SOTP is a downside anchor ($2.3-3.4T, or $157-234 a share before net cash), not a price target: it shows the size of the ecosystem premium an investor is buying.
rows.confidence: medium — segment revenue and gross profit are derived from filed data, but the opex allocation and multiple choice are assumptions.
rows.follow_up: What would Services be worth at 20x EV/Sales if 20% of its revenue is a Google payment that a court could remove?

rows.finding: Apple's P/E was 24.6x at FY2022 year-end, 27.9x at FY2023, 37.5x at FY2024, 34.2x at FY2025 and 39.5x on 2026-10-30; the ten-year mean is 25.35x, the five-year average 30.2x, the five-year range 22.1-40.6x and the current multiple sits at the 100th percentile of it. From 2022-09-24 to 2026-10-30 the share price rose 129% while diluted EPS rose 43%, so about half the return came from the multiple.
rows.mechanism: Re-rating against a rising discount rate did the work: the ten-year Treasury yield rose 84bp in the last twelve months to 4.93%, yet Apple's multiple expanded, which cannot be repeated indefinitely because the earnings yield is already below the Treasury.
rows.benchmark: Its own ten-year mean of 25.35x and five-year range of 22.1-40.6x; S&P 500 trailing 21.76x.
rows.weakens: The EPS base is flattered: FY2025's 22.7% EPS growth becomes 10.4% normalising the Irish tax charge, and the June 2026 gross margin contained about two points of tariff refunds.
rows.implication: Future returns must come from earnings, not from multiple expansion; a return to the five-year average multiple alone would put the shares near $296.
rows.confidence: high — fiscal-year multiples are computed from filed EPS and closing prices, and the history is corroborated by two independent trackers.
rows.follow_up: How much of the 2024-2026 re-rating survives if the ten-year yield stays near 5%?

rows.finding: The last filed results are Q3 FY2026 (2026-06-27): revenue $109.4B, +16.4%, gross margin 50.1% including about two points of tariff refunds, EPS $2.02 +29%; fiscal Q4 revenue is guided to +9-11% with results due 2026-11-02. The sell-side consensus target is $339.35 across 50 analysts and the 43-analyst range is $245-$405, so the 2026-10-30 price is at or above the average target.
rows.mechanism: The price has run past the average analyst target, so the Q4 event carries asymmetric risk: a beat is already partly priced, while a guide below +9% would remove the growth the reverse DCF requires.
rows.benchmark: Consensus $339.35 versus $344.63 price; the low target of $245 is within 1% of the 52-week low of $243.42.
rows.weakens: Consensus targets lag price in momentum cycles and the dispersion is wide ($245-$405, a 65% spread), so the average target is a sentiment read, not a valuation.
rows.implication: No analyst cushion into 2026-11-02; a long-only fund should let the print pass before establishing a position.
rows.confidence: medium — two independent trackers, but they disagree on sample size and median, and Apple's guidance is an analyst aggregation rather than a company point guide.
rows.follow_up: Does the Q4 release confirm the +9-11% revenue guide and a gross margin above 48% ex-refunds?

rows.finding: Capital return: quarterly dividend $0.27 (0.31% yield), a new $100B buyback authorised in April 2026, $82.2B of repurchases and $15.6B of dividends in the trailing twelve months, a total shareholder yield of 1.9% against a peer median of 0.5%, and diluted shares down from 16,865M in FY2021 to 14,715M in Q3 FY2026 (-12.7%).
rows.mechanism: At 39.5x, each dollar of buyback retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield, below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, so the repurchase supports EPS but is not obviously accretive to value per share; at 25x the same dollar would yield 4.0%.
rows.benchmark: Peer median total shareholder yield 0.5%; Apple 1.9%; ten-year Treasury 4.93%.
rows.weakens: The buyback still retires about 1.6% of the shares a year and the $100B authorisation is about 2% of market value, so capital return is a real bid under the stock; the dividend has been raised annually.
rows.implication: Capital return is a floor under EPS and a partial exit route for holders, not a source of return at today's multiple.
rows.confidence: high — buyback and dividend cash flows are from the filed cash-flow statement and the authorisation from the April 2026 release.
rows.follow_up: Will Apple re-authorise at the same $100B pace in 2027 if free cash flow normalises toward $110B?

plan.decision_question: What is Apple worth on 2026-10-30, and what revenue growth, margin and terminal assumptions does the $344.63 close already discount?
plan.thesis_sentence: At $344.63 on NasdaqGS (2026-10-30 close) Apple is priced at 39.5x trailing earnings, 35.2x forward earnings and a 2.7% free-cash-flow yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a price that requires roughly 11-12% annual free-cash-flow growth for a decade — several times what its device markets or its own last four years delivered — so the watchlist case turns on the entry price that restores a margin of safety, not on whether Apple is a good business.
plan.why_different: The financial analysis measures the quality of the earnings; this section converts those same statements and prices into what the buyer is paying for them: implied growth, peer-relative premium, sum-of-the-parts discount and the entry band that follows.
plan.mechanism: At 39.5x the earnings yield is 2.5% versus 4.93% on the ten-year Treasury, and the reverse DCF already assumes the FCF multiple halves to 18.7x by 2036, so the price can only be earned through double-digit FCF growth from the Services mix and an iPhone cycle, not from further re-rating; each buyback dollar retires stock at 2.5%, below the risk-free yield.
plan.comparison_set: MSFT 27.3x, GOOGL 14.6x, META 21.0x (peer median 21.0x), Samsung 12.5x; S&P 500 18.40x forward and 21.76x trailing; Apple's own ten-year mean P/E of 25.35x, five-year range 22.1-40.6x, and FY2021-FY2025 FCF CAGR of 1.5%.
plan.counter_evidence: Apple's 2.7% FCF yield is the highest of the four mega-caps because capital expenditure is $10B against hyperscaler AI budgets, and if the AI iPhone cycle lifts revenue 10%+ for several years while Services compounds at 14% on a 76% gross margin, a 35x forward multiple can be earned rather than merely re-rated.
plan.visual: Valuation methods table (reverse DCF at four growth rates plus sum of the parts) with the peer multiples table beside it.
plan.prohibited: cheap or expensive with no mechanism; 'priced for perfection'; 'margin of safety' without a number; 'the market is always right'; any statement about how the section is written.

rows.finding: There is no plausible takeover exit: Apple's market value is $5,029.6B, so the largest technology acquisition ever ($68.7B) equals 1.4% of it, and any bid would face US and EU antitrust review of a platform with 23.6% of global smartphone shipments.
rows.mechanism: With no strategic buyer able to pay a control premium, the exit price is the market multiple on the day of sale, which makes the entry multiple the dominant term in the return.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft's $68.7B all-cash acquisition of Activision Blizzard (2022-01-18), the largest technology deal on record, which took about 18 months and a divestiture to clear regulators.
rows.weakens: A mega-cap can still be broken up by regulators or acquired in parts, and a very large cash-rich acquirer could pay up for a division; the 1.4% comparison is about a whole-company bid.
rows.implication: Value can only be realised by selling into the market; the takeover premium is effectively zero and should not be modelled.
rows.confidence: high — the deal value is from the announcement and Apple's market capitalisation from dated market data.
rows.follow_up: Could a sovereign wealth fund or strategic investor build a stake large enough to influence strategy, and would CFIUS review apply?

rows.finding: Apple's four large drawdowns were 2018 -36.73% ($58.02 on 2018-10-03 to $36.71 on 2018-12-24), 2020 -31.43% ($81.80 to $56.09, 40 days), 2022 -30.75% ($182.01 to $126.04, 359 days) and 2025 -30.22% ($247.10 to $172.42, 43 days); the ten-year average intra-year drawdown is -21.4% over 82 days, and each was recovered within the following year (2020 +80.75%, 2025 +8.56% for the calendar year).
rows.mechanism: Apple's drawdowns were multiple compressions on intact franchises, so the recovery came from a re-rating as much as from earnings; at 39.5x there is little multiple room left to power the next recovery.
rows.benchmark: Apple's ten-year average intra-year drawdown of -21.4%, average 82 days peak-to-trough.
rows.weakens: Every one of those recoveries happened while the multiple was expanding on falling or near-zero real rates; a repeat at a 39.5x starting multiple would require earnings growth alone to do the work.
rows.implication: Size the position for a 20-30% drawdown as the normal case: from $344.63 the average drawdown is about $271 and a 30% drawdown about $241.
rows.confidence: high — a daily close series with peak and trough dates for each year.
rows.follow_up: Does the 2026 cycle repeat the pattern if memory costs and a slowing iPhone cycle coincide?

rows.finding: The last two big buying opportunities came at 17-21x earnings: $126.04 at the 2022 trough was 20.6x FY2022 EPS of $6.11, and $56.09 at the 2020 trough was about 17.1x FY2020 EPS of $3.28; $344.63 is 39.5x trailing EPS of $8.72 and 35.2x forward EPS of about $9.79.
rows.mechanism: The trough multiple, not the trough price, is what made those purchases work: the same 20x on today's much larger EPS is a far higher price, which is why a price band must be set on the multiple rather than on the old share price.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own entry multiples: 20.6x on FY2022 EPS at the 2022 trough and 17.1x on FY2020 EPS at the 2020 trough, against 39.5x today.
rows.weakens: Apple's earnings and cash flow are 40% larger than in 2022, so a 20x multiple on today's EPS is not the same business; the lower multiple may simply never return for a company with 76%-margin Services.
rows.implication: Waiting for a repeat of 17-21x means waiting for a price near $174-215 and may mean never owning the stock; the practical compromise is a 25-30x band.
rows.confidence: medium — trough prices are dated closes and the EPS are fiscal-year diluted figures, so the trough multiple is approximate.
rows.follow_up: Would a 20x multiple on today's EPS ($174) ever be reached without a genuine earnings recession?

rows.finding: Return sensitivity to entry: at $344.63 a three-year exit at 25x earns about -3.3% a year, at 30x +2.7% and at 35x +8.2%; at $296 the same exits earn +1.8%, +8.1% and +13.8%; at $248 they earn +8.0%, +14.8% and +21%+.
rows.mechanism: The entry multiple sets the arithmetic: paying 35x for 8% EPS growth and exiting at 25x loses money even though the business grows, while paying 25x for the same growth and exiting at 25x earns the growth plus the dividend.
rows.benchmark: An 8% annual equity hurdle for a long-only fund; EPS growth of 8% a year from $9.79 to $12.33 by fiscal 2029.
rows.weakens: If EPS compounds at 12-16% as it did in FY2026, every row improves by roughly 4-8 points a year and today's price could clear the hurdle.
rows.implication: Only at or below about $296 does a long-only fund earn its hurdle without relying on the multiple staying at a five-year high; at $344.63 the return depends on a 35x exit.
rows.confidence: medium — arithmetic, but the EPS path and exit multiple are assumptions, not forecasts.
rows.follow_up: What EPS growth does the FY2027 consensus imply, and does it survive a normalised tax rate and a 48% gross margin?

rows.finding: The Google search-distribution payment — reported at about $20B a year, never disclosed by Apple — is roughly 17% of Services revenue and 22% of services gross profit; the default-payment ban took effect in June 2026 under the April 2026 remedy order, with choice screens required.
rows.mechanism: The payment is almost pure margin with no capital attached, so losing it hits earnings and the multiple at the same time — the same policy risk that the valuation section capitalises at 39.5x.
rows.benchmark: Services revenue of $120.5B TTM and services gross profit of $91.6B; a 76.0% services gross margin.
rows.weakens: The deal may survive in restricted, non-exclusive form and is under appeal; Apple's Q3 FY2026 Services revenue still grew 12.1%, so no loss is visible in the filed results yet.
rows.implication: A sell trigger: if the payment is lost without an offset, about 9% of market value at a 30x multiple is at risk, so position size must survive that hit.
rows.confidence: medium — the payment size is a reported estimate Apple has never confirmed, and the remedy is under appeal.
rows.follow_up: What share of the Q3 FY2026 Services growth of 12.1% came from the search payment, and what does Apple disclose about the outcome of the appeal?

rows.finding: Liquidity is not a constraint: Apple trades $13.84B a day (20-day average, 40.41M shares) and the company itself retires about 1.6% of shares a year ($82.2B of repurchases), while a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, under 0.1% of one day's volume.
rows.mechanism: Deep liquidity plus a continuous buyback bid means the cost of exiting is the multiple at the moment of sale, not market impact, which shifts the design of the exit from execution to valuation triggers.
rows.benchmark: Apple's $13.84B average daily traded value over 20 days; $82.2B of trailing-twelve-month buybacks, 1.6% of market value.
rows.weakens: Liquidity evaporates in stress: in the 2025 episode the stock fell 30% in 43 days, and the buyback is discretionary and can slow, as it did when repurchases fell to $62.1B in nine months from $70.6B.
rows.implication: The exit is a price decision, not a liquidity decision: a long-only fund can sell in a day, but the drawdown record says it will not want to.
rows.confidence: high — volume and buyback figures are dated and filed.
rows.follow_up: How does liquidity behave in a 2025-style 43-day, 30% drawdown, and what slippage should a 5% position assume?

plan.decision_question: For a long-only fund, at what price does Apple become a starter and then a full position, what forces a sale, and what total return should the holder expect at each entry price?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple offers no takeover or listing exit — at a $5.03T market value the largest technology acquisition on record would be 1.4% of the company — so the only exit is a sale into a deep but volatile market, and the discipline has to be a price band: a first tranche at $275-300 (28-31x forward earnings), a full position at or below $250 (about 25x, the ten-year mean), and a sale if Services growth falls below 5% or the gross margin below 44%, because at 39.5x a 21% average drawdown is the normal cost of owning it.
plan.why_different: The valuation section asks what the company is worth; this section asks how a holder gets paid and how a holder gets out, using the drawdown record, the entry multiple and named policy tests rather than a price target.
plan.mechanism: For a listed mega-cap the exit is the market's bid, so the return is set by the entry multiple and the holding period: buybacks and dividends add about 1.9% a year, too little to offset a de-rating from 35x to 25x, so the entry band and the sale triggers do the work that an acquisition or IPO would do for a private company.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own four drawdowns (2018 -36.73%, 2020 -31.43%, 2022 -30.75%, 2025 -30.22%; ten-year average -21.4% over 82 days), the S&P 500 at -3.05% and Nasdaq-100 at -9.09% from their highs on 2026-10-30, and the largest technology acquisition ($68.7B) as the takeover benchmark.
plan.counter_evidence: A 30x-plus multiple may never offer a margin of safety again: if Services keeps compounding at 14% and the buyback retires 1.6% a year, waiting for $250 could mean never owning the best cash generator in the market, so the cost of the discipline is opportunity rather than loss.
plan.visual: Exit routes table and the entry-price/exit-multiple return sensitivity table, with the drawdown history table beside them.
plan.prohibited: IPO or trade sale as a realistic exit; 'buy and hold forever' with no triggers; vague 'long term'; 'the stock always comes back' without the multiple at which it came back.

rows.mechanism: With no strategic buyer able to pay a control premium, the exit price is the market multiple on the day of sale, which makes the entry multiple the dominant term in the return.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft's $68.7B all-cash acquisition of Activision Blizzard (2022-01-18), the largest technology deal on record, which took about 18 months and a divestiture to clear regulators.
rows.weakens: A mega-cap can still be broken up by regulators or acquired in parts, and a very large cash-rich acquirer could pay up for a division; the 1.4% comparison is about a whole-company bid.
rows.implication: Value can only be realised by selling into the market; the takeover premium is effectively zero and should not be modelled.
rows.confidence: high — the deal value is from the announcement and Apple's market capitalisation from dated market data.
rows.follow_up: Could a sovereign wealth fund or strategic investor build a stake large enough to influence strategy, and would CFIUS review apply?

rows.finding: Apple's four large drawdowns were 2018 -36.73% ($58.02 on 2018-10-03 to $36.71 on 2018-12-24), 2020 -31.43% ($81.80 to $56.09, 40 days), 2022 -30.75% ($182.01 to $126.04, 359 days) and 2025 -30.22% ($247.10 to $172.42, 43 days); the ten-year average intra-year drawdown is -21.4% over 82 days, and each was recovered within the following year (2020 +80.75%, 2025 +8.56% for the calendar year).
rows.mechanism: Apple's drawdowns were multiple compressions on intact franchises, so the recovery came from a re-rating as much as from earnings; at 39.5x there is little multiple room left to power the next recovery.
rows.benchmark: Apple's ten-year average intra-year drawdown of -21.4%, average 82 days peak-to-trough.
rows.weakens: Every one of those recoveries happened while the multiple was expanding on falling or near-zero real rates; a repeat at a 39.5x starting multiple would require earnings growth alone to do the work.
rows.implication: Size the position for a 20-30% drawdown as the normal case: from $344.63 the average drawdown is about $271 and a 30% drawdown about $241.
rows.confidence: high — a daily close series with peak and trough dates for each year.
rows.follow_up: Does the 2026 cycle repeat the pattern if memory costs and a slowing iPhone cycle coincide?

rows.finding: The last two big buying opportunities came at 17-21x earnings: $126.04 at the 2022 trough was 20.6x FY2022 EPS of $6.11, and $56.09 at the 2020 trough was about 17.1x FY2020 EPS of $3.28; $344.63 is 39.5x trailing EPS of $8.72 and 35.2x forward EPS of about $9.79.
rows.mechanism: The trough multiple, not the trough price, is what made those purchases work: the same 20x on today's much larger EPS is a far higher price, which is why a price band must be set on the multiple rather than on the old share price.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own entry multiples: 20.6x on FY2022 EPS at the 2022 trough and 17.1x on FY2020 EPS at the 2020 trough, against 39.5x today.
rows.weakens: Apple's earnings and cash flow are 40% larger than in 2022, so a 20x multiple on today's EPS is not the same business; the lower multiple may simply never return for a company with 76%-margin Services.
rows.implication: Waiting for a repeat of 17-21x means waiting for a price near $174-215 and may mean never owning the stock; the practical compromise is a 25-30x band.
rows.confidence: medium — trough prices are dated closes and the EPS are fiscal-year diluted figures, so the trough multiple is approximate.
rows.follow_up: Would a 20x multiple on today's EPS ($174) ever be reached without a genuine earnings recession?

rows.finding: Return sensitivity to entry: at $344.63 a three-year exit at 25x earns about -3.3% a year, at 30x +2.7% and at 35x +8.2%; at $296 the same exits earn +1.8%, +8.1% and +13.8%; at $248 they earn +8.0%, +14.8% and +21%+.
rows.mechanism: The entry multiple sets the arithmetic: paying 35x for 8% EPS growth and exiting at 25x loses money even though the business grows, while paying 25x for the same growth and exiting at 25x earns the growth plus the dividend.
rows.benchmark: An 8% annual equity hurdle for a long-only fund; EPS growth of 8% a year from $9.79 to $12.33 by fiscal 2029.
rows.weakens: If EPS compounds at 12-16% as it did in FY2026, every row improves by roughly 4-8 points a year and today's price could clear the hurdle.
rows.implication: Only at or below about $296 does a long-only fund earn its hurdle without relying on the multiple staying at a five-year high; at $344.63 the return depends on a 35x exit.
rows.confidence: medium — arithmetic, but the EPS path and exit multiple are assumptions, not forecasts.
rows.follow_up: What EPS growth does the FY2027 consensus imply, and does it survive a normalised tax rate and a 48% gross margin?

rows.finding: The Google search payment, reported at $20B in 2022 (the latest figure in testimony) and never disclosed by Apple, is about 17% of trailing Services revenue of $120.5B and 22% of services gross profit of $91.6B. The D.D.C.'s 2025-09-02 remedies decision refused the DOJ's proposed near-total ban on distribution payments and instead barred exclusive contracts while permitting default-placement payments not conditioned on exclusivity and running one year or less; final judgment was entered in December 2025, Google appealed in January 2026, the DOJ and states cross-appealed in February 2026, and the appeals were pending at 2026-10-29.
rows.mechanism: The payment survives on annually renegotiable, non-exclusive terms, so its value depends on renewal economics and the appeal rather than on a ban already in force; because it is almost pure margin, a cut hits earnings and the multiple together.
rows.benchmark: Services revenue $120.5B TTM; services gross profit $91.6B at a 76.0% gross margin.
rows.weakens: A competing independent report claimed an April 2026 order banned the payment from June 2026; the CRS analysis of the September 2025 decision and Alphabet's 10-Q legal note contradict it, and no primary record shows such a ban.
rows.implication: Sell trigger: loss or material cut of the payment at the one-year renewal or on appeal without an offsetting services gain; about 9% of market value at 30x is at risk.
rows.confidence: high on the remedy status and appeal timeline (primary court analysis and Alphabet's filed legal proceedings); medium on the $20B payment size, which Apple has never disclosed.
rows.follow_up: What does Apple receive at the first one-year renewal, and how much of Services growth does it explain?

rows.finding: Liquidity is not a constraint: Apple trades $13.84B a day (20-day average, 40.41M shares) and the company itself retires about 1.6% of shares a year ($82.2B of repurchases), while a 1% position in a $1B fund is $10M, under 0.1% of one day's volume.
rows.mechanism: Deep liquidity plus a continuous buyback bid means the cost of exiting is the multiple at the moment of sale, not market impact, which shifts the design of the exit from execution to valuation triggers.
rows.benchmark: Apple's $13.84B average daily traded value over 20 days; $82.2B of trailing-twelve-month buybacks, 1.6% of market value.
rows.weakens: Liquidity evaporates in stress: in the 2025 episode the stock fell 30% in 43 days, and the buyback is discretionary and can slow, as it did when repurchases fell to $62.1B in nine months from $70.6B.
rows.implication: The exit is a price decision, not a liquidity decision: a long-only fund can sell in a day, but the drawdown record says it will not want to.
rows.confidence: high — volume and buyback figures are dated and filed.
rows.follow_up: How does liquidity behave in a 2025-style 43-day, 30% drawdown, and what slippage should a 5% position assume?

plan.decision_question: For a long-only fund, at what price does Apple become a starter and then a full position, what forces a sale, and what total return should the holder expect at each entry price?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple offers no takeover or listing exit — at a $5.03T market value the largest technology acquisition on record would be 1.4% of the company — so the only exit is a sale into a deep but volatile market, and the discipline has to be a price band: a first tranche at $275-296 (28-30x forward earnings), a full position at or below $250 (about 25x, the ten-year mean), and a sale if Services growth falls below 5% or the gross margin below 44%, because at 39.5x a 21% average drawdown is the normal cost of owning it.
plan.why_different: The valuation section asks what the company is worth; this section asks how a holder gets paid and how a holder gets out, using the drawdown record, the entry multiple and named policy tests rather than a price target.
plan.mechanism: For a listed mega-cap the exit is the market's bid, so the return is set by the entry multiple and the holding period: buybacks and dividends add about 1.9% a year, too little to offset a de-rating from 35x to 25x, so the entry band and the sale triggers do the work that an acquisition or IPO would do for a private company.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own four drawdowns (2018 -36.73%, 2020 -31.43%, 2022 -30.75%, 2025 -30.22%; ten-year average -21.4% over 82 days), the S&P 500 at -3.05% and Nasdaq-100 at -9.09% from their highs on 2026-10-30, and the largest technology acquisition ($68.7B) as the takeover benchmark.
plan.counter_evidence: A 30x-plus multiple may never offer a margin of safety again: if Services keeps compounding at 14% and the buyback retires 1.6% a year, waiting for $250 could mean never owning the best cash generator in the market, so the cost of the discipline is opportunity rather than loss.
plan.visual: Exit routes table and the entry-price/exit-multiple return sensitivity table, with the drawdown history table beside them.
plan.prohibited: IPO or trade sale as a realistic exit; 'buy and hold forever' with no triggers; vague 'long term'; 'the stock always comes back' without the multiple at which it came back.

rows.finding: FY2025 EX-21 lists 19 subsidiaries including three Irish entities (Apple Operations International, Apple Operations Limited, Apple Distribution International); Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe, the entities named in the 2016 Commission decision, are absent. Foreign pretax earnings were $82.0bn of $132.7bn (61.8%) in FY2025; the effective tax rate was 15.6%.
rows.mechanism: Profit booked outside the U.S. at 5.4pp below the 21% statutory rate raises after-tax cash flow, but entity-level profit is undisclosed, so the durability of the tax structure cannot be tested from the filings.
rows.benchmark: U.S. statutory rate 21%; Apple's own effective rate 14.7% FY2023, 24.1% FY2024 (state-aid charge), 15.6% FY2025.
rows.weakens: The 10-K gives no entity-level income, ownership percentages or transfer-pricing detail; EX-21 omits subsidiaries that are not significant.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise the 15.6% rate as permanent; require the Irish CRO accounts and transfer-pricing disclosure before underwriting it.
rows.confidence: medium: filing facts high, role of each Irish entity inferred from the pre-2015 structure.
rows.follow_up: Which entity books non-U.S. profit, and what effective rate applies under Pillar Two from FY2026?

rows.finding: EC state-aid decision 2016-08-30 (up to €13bn); General Court annulled it 2020-07-15; the ECJ set that aside and confirmed the decision 2024-09-10; Apple recorded a $10.2bn net Q4 FY2024 charge, paying $15.8bn to Ireland by releasing escrow, offset by a $4.8bn U.S. foreign tax credit and $823m of unrecognised tax benefits.
rows.mechanism: A retroactive liability equal to 11.9% of one year's pretax income shows tax rulings can be clawed back with interest, raising the discount rate applied to non-U.S. profit.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 pretax income $132.7bn; the $15.8bn recovery equals 11.9% of it.
rows.weakens: Ireland changed its law effective January 2015, eliminating the tax opinions; no comparable live case is disclosed.
rows.implication: Price a policy tail on the tax rate; the legal precedent is now settled against the company.
rows.confidence: high: dates and amounts from the 10-K.
rows.follow_up: Is any Pillar Two top-up tax or new EU transfer-pricing challenge outstanding?

rows.finding: 14,594,180,000 shares outstanding at 2026-07-17 versus 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02; 215m shares repurchased for $61.8bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus $70.6bn in the prior-year period; a $100bn programme was authorised on 2025-05-01; cash and securities of $146.5bn against $84.3bn of debt gives about $62.2bn net cash at 2026-06-27; market capitalisation $5.03tn on 2026-10-30.
rows.mechanism: Buybacks shrink the count about 0.7% in 6.5 months, but the dollar pace fell 12% year on year as the share price rose, so repurchase price discipline matters more at a $5tn capitalisation.
rows.benchmark: Nine-month FY2025 repurchases $70.6bn; 215m shares equal about 1.5% of the count in nine months.
rows.weakens: The company discloses no intrinsic-value estimate; buybacks can still be EPS-accretive even at high prices.
rows.implication: Treat capital allocation, not liquidity, as the balance-sheet risk at 2026 prices; track average repurchase price.
rows.confidence: high on figures; medium on the capital-allocation judgement.
rows.follow_up: What average price did Apple pay in FY2026, and how much of the $100bn authorisation remains?

rows.finding: One class of common stock ($0.00001 par) with votes tracking economics; 7 of 9 directors independent after 2026-09-01; directors and officers hold 9,079,765 shares (0.06%); Vanguard 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%; Levinson drew 9.0% opposition and say-on-pay 8.6% opposition at the 2026-02-24 annual meeting; a 'China Entanglement Audit' shareholder proposal won 1.4%.
rows.mechanism: Without dual-class stock votes equal economics, but inside ownership below 1% makes alignment depend on pay design and reputation rather than ownership; a chair since 2000 attracts the largest protest vote.
rows.benchmark: Nasdaq requires a majority-independent board (7/9 = 78% against a 50% rule); no independent benchmark for say-on-pay was retrieved.
rows.weakens: Cook holds 3,280,295 shares, worth over $1bn at the 2026-10-30 market capitalisation, so his personal alignment is material despite the low group percentage.
rows.implication: Alignment is professional, not ownership-based; board refresh and succession at the chair are legitimate governance asks.
rows.confidence: high.
rows.follow_up: Will the board add AI and regulatory expertise and set a chair retirement age?

rows.finding: FY2025 net sales $416.2bn (+6%); nine-month FY2026 net sales $364.4bn (+16%), Services $91.7bn (+14%) and Greater China $64.8bn (+30%); FY2025 Services gross margin 75.4% and total gross margin 46.9%; Q3 FY2026 gross margin $54.8bn on $109.4bn of sales (50.1%).
rows.mechanism: Growth is iPhone-led with a high-margin Services attach to an installed base above 2.5bn devices; the China rebound and services mix lifted gross margin above 50% in Q3 FY2026.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 Greater China sales $64.4bn (−4%) and total gross margin 46.9%.
rows.weakens: The 10-Q warns of component cost inflation in advanced semiconductors, NAND and DRAM and of tariff changes, so the 2026 margin may be cyclical.
rows.implication: Operating leverage is real but partly cyclical; underwrite a margin range, not the Q3 peak.
rows.confidence: high on figures; medium on margin durability.
rows.follow_up: How much of FY2026 growth is units versus price, and what memory-cost headwind hits FY2027?

rows.finding: DOJ filed a civil antitrust suit on 2024-03-21 in the District of New Jersey seeking equitable relief; on 2025-04-30 the California court found Apple in violation of the 2021 Epic injunction, barred fees on out-of-app purchases and referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt; the EU fined Apple €500m under the DMA on 2025-04-23, which Apple appealed.
rows.mechanism: Remedies forcing alternative distribution and payment could compress the 75.4%-gross-margin Services line, which produced 39.1% of nine-month FY2026 gross profit ($70.0bn of $178.8bn).
rows.benchmark: Services was 25.2% of nine-month FY2026 revenue but 39.1% of gross profit.
rows.weakens: The DOJ seeks equitable relief, not damages; Apple says it has substantial defences; any remedy is years away.
rows.implication: Underwrite the Services margin, not the fines, as the antitrust exposure.
rows.confidence: high on facts; medium on remedy impact.
rows.follow_up: What remedy scope and timetable does the New Jersey court signal for 2027?
