plan.decision_question: Is Apple's corporate, ownership and capital structure as clean and shareholder-aligned as the equity story assumes?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's structure is clean in law — one share class, a majority-independent board and net cash — but not in economics: 61.8% of pretax profit is booked outside the U.S. at a 15.6% effective rate, insiders own 0.06%, and the same director has chaired the board since 2000, so 'alignment' rests on pay design and a tax structure the EU has already litigated once.
plan.why_different: Other sections price the business, market and product; this one audits the container — which entities hold the profit, who controls the votes, and how capital is returned.
plan.mechanism: The legal and tax structure sets after-tax cash flow and policy tail risk; the ownership and board structure determines whose interests capital allocation serves.
plan.comparison_set: Apple's own 2023-2025 effective tax rates, FY2025 versus FY2026 buyback pace, and the Nasdaq majority-independent board rule.
plan.counter_evidence: The tax structure survived the ECJ in 2024; Cook's 3.28m shares make his alignment material; buybacks and services have compounded per-share value for a decade.
plan.visual: kpi table, 15-row timeline and legal-entity table
plan.prohibited: clean structure, shareholder-aligned without evidence, huge, strong, well positioned, many

rows.finding: The board appointed John Ternus CEO effective 2026-09-01, with Tim Cook as executive chair and Arthur Levinson as lead independent director; Ternus, 50, joined Apple in 2001, became VP Hardware Engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021, and has no disclosed CEO or P&L role before 2026.
rows.mechanism: An internal hardware engineer preserves product-integration culture, but value is migrating to software, AI and services at the moment he takes over.
rows.benchmark: Apple's 2011 Jobs-to-Cook transition, also an internal promotion; Ternus is Apple's eighth CEO.
rows.weakens: Ternus's product record (iPad, AirPods, iPhone 17/Air, MacBook Neo), a unanimous board and a five-month handover argue for continuity.
rows.implication: Succession risk is lower than feared but renewal risk is higher: the new CEO has never allocated capital or answered to public markets.
rows.confidence: high: appointment, date and biography from the 8-K and company release.
rows.follow_up: What operating authority does Cook retain as executive chair, and what is Ternus's CEO compensation?

rows.finding: John Giannandrea stepped down as AI chief on 2025-12-01 after Siri's delay; Amar Subramanya (ex-Microsoft corporate VP of AI, 16 years at Google and head of engineering for Gemini Assistant) became VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi; Apple announced a multiyear deal on 2026-01-12 to use Google Gemini for the Siri upgrade due in 2026.
rows.mechanism: Apple is buying frontier capability from a competitor while rebuilding internal leadership: faster than building, but it weakens differentiation and gives Google leverage.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft-OpenAI and Google DeepMind own frontier models; Apple had pursued in-house AI since 2018.
rows.weakens: Federighi's software record, Subramanya's Gemini experience and Apple's distribution still give it the fastest route to mass-market AI.
rows.implication: Underwrite AI as a feature that protects hardware replacement, not as a new profit pool, until Apple discloses model economics.
rows.confidence: high on facts; medium on competitive consequence.
rows.follow_up: What are the Gemini deal terms, and is Apple training a frontier model in parallel?

rows.finding: Srouji became chief hardware officer combining silicon and hardware engineering; Federighi holds software plus AI; Cue added health to services; Parekh has been CFO since 2025-01-01; Khan COO since 2025-07; Newstead GC from 2026-03-01; O'Brien runs retail and people. Most of the executive team has spent 20+ years at Apple, and two people carry the silicon and AI remits.
rows.mechanism: Concentrating silicon in Srouji and software/AI in Federighi creates key-person risk in exactly the two capabilities the transition depends on.
rows.benchmark: The 2011-2023 team was near-static; four senior roles (CFO, COO, GC, AI) changed in 2025-2026.
rows.weakens: Deep internal pipeline and Srouji's expanded remit give one accountable owner for hardware.
rows.implication: Diligence should ask for named deputies in silicon and AI; key-person risk is the team's main discount.
rows.confidence: high on roles; medium on the key-person judgement.
rows.follow_up: Who are Srouji's and Federighi's deputies, and are retention packages in place?

rows.finding: Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m (base $3m unchanged since 2016, cash incentive at 200% of base, $50m equity target), positioned in the 80th-90th percentile of peer CEO pay; other named executives target $1m base, 200% cash and $20m equity; Parekh's target was $16.75m; the CEO ownership guideline is 10x salary; say-on-pay drew 8.6% opposition on 2026-02-24.
rows.mechanism: Pay is peer-benchmarked high but equity-heavy, which retains executives through a multiyear transition; the 8.6% protest signals some shareholder discomfort.
rows.benchmark: 80th-90th percentile of the primary peer group, as disclosed by the company.
rows.weakens: 8.6% opposition is not a crisis but is above routine approval; CEO pay is immaterial to a $5tn market value.
rows.implication: Pay is a weak signal for the investment case; retaining Srouji and Federighi matters more than the level.
rows.confidence: high.
rows.follow_up: How is Ternus's CEO pay structured, and does it carry AI and China metrics?

rows.finding: Planned transitions replaced the CFO (Maestri to Parekh, effective 2025-01-01), COO (Williams to Khan, 2025-07), general counsel (Adams to Newstead, effective 2026-03-01), AI chief (Giannandrea to Subramanya, 2025-12-01) and CEO (Cook to Ternus, 2026-09-01) within 24 months.
rows.mechanism: Staggered, pre-announced transitions preserve continuity, but the whole C-suite turned over while AI and antitrust pressure intensified.
rows.benchmark: Apple's prior decade had almost no C-suite turnover.
rows.weakens: All were planned successions rather than resignations; Newstead and Subramanya bring external experience.
rows.implication: Execution risk lies in coordination, not departures; the first 12 months of Ternus's team are the test.
rows.confidence: high.
rows.follow_up: Has any 2026 departure not been pre-announced, particularly in design after Williams retired?

rows.finding: Cook (Auburn 1982, Duke MBA 1988; 12 years at IBM, then Compaq) is the operator and policy face; Ternus the product engineer; Srouji the silicon builder; Federighi the software and AI owner; Cue the services monetiser; Parekh the finance disciplinarian. No board member has operating frontier-AI experience.
rows.mechanism: Apple's model rewards integration across silicon, software and services; the division of labour matches that model but leaves no frontier-AI owner at CEO or board level.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft's Satya Nadella (engineering and cloud) and Google's Sundar Pichai (product) versus a hardware engineer as Apple CEO.
rows.weakens: The board's aerospace (Austin) and pharmaceutical (Gorsky) experience may be more relevant to manufacturing and health than to AI.
rows.implication: The missing hire is not a CFO but a credible AI product leader with executive authority; Subramanya is VP-level and not on the executive team.
rows.confidence: medium.
rows.follow_up: Will Subramanya be elevated to the executive team, and will the board add AI expertise?

rows.finding: Apple guided fiscal Q4 2026 gross margin to 47-48% including about 1 point of tariff refunds, i.e. roughly 46-47% ex-refunds against 48.1% ex-refund in the June quarter, with consensus revenue of about $113.3bn and EPS of about $1.99.
rows.mechanism: The company itself prices the memory cost transfer into the next quarter's margin: a 2.1-3.1 point sequential decline, and a lower underlying margin than a year earlier once the refund is stripped out, which is the opposite of a new 50% floor.
rows.benchmark: June 2026 quarter 50.1% reported and 48.1% ex-refund; fiscal 2025 full-year 46.9%; fiscal 2023 44.1%.
rows.weakens: The thesis-table reading that FY2027 consensus EPS of $9.79 is a reasonable base case unadjusted.
rows.implication: Trailing EPS of $8.72 is a margin peak, not a run-rate; the base-case forward EPS of $9.79 needs margin to stabilise before FY2027 begins. Price the entry band lower.
rows.confidence: medium - company guidance confirmed by a specialist preview; the ex-refund split is a calculation on Apple's own disclosure
rows.follow_up: Does the December-quarter guide on 2026-11-02 imply gross margin below 46% ex-refund?

rows.finding: DRAM sufficiency ratio of -1% to -2% in 2026, a widening supply-demand gap in 2027, meaningful new capacity only in the second half of 2027 and substantial output not before 2028; consumer device shipments fall again in 2027.
rows.mechanism: HBM and AI-server demand crowd out commodity DRAM, so the three suppliers keep pricing power over handset makers for another eighteen months; that fixes Apple's cost base while its service annuity price is fixed, compressing the blended margin.
rows.benchmark: IDC's 2028 normalisation for device pools; Apple's own 10-Q statement that component constraints and costs are expected to intensify.
rows.weakens: The base-case driver that margin gives back about a point and then settles.
rows.implication: A one-point give-back is optimistic; model two to four points through FY2027 and test the buy band against $8.20-8.90 of EPS.
rows.confidence: high for 2027 DRAM tightness; medium for the size of the margin hit, which depends on price pass-through not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What iPhone 18 Pro price increase does Apple announce for 2027, and does volume hold?

rows.finding: China smartphone shipments fell 15.4% to 57.9m units in Q3 2026, a sixth straight decline; Apple's own units fell 4.3% while its share rose to 17.8% from 15.8%; Huawei shipped 12.2m units for about 21% share and grew 17.3%.
rows.mechanism: In a shrinking market share gains come from rivals' exits, not from demand: Apple's 30% Greater China revenue growth in nine months of FY2026 was price, mix and currency on falling units, so the line mean-reverts once the price comparison laps.
rows.benchmark: Greater China revenue $64.8bn in nine months of FY2026 against $49.9bn a year earlier; Apple share 18.1% in Q2 2026 and 17.8% in Q3 2026; Huawei 22.6% in Q2.
rows.weakens: The market section's framing of China growth as a competitive win rather than a price and mix effect.
rows.implication: China is a 17.8% revenue line with declining volume; a 20% revenue fall removes about 4% of net income, and the FY2027 comparison is against a +30% base.
rows.confidence: high on the IDC data, medium on the revenue elasticity
rows.follow_up: What does the December-quarter China revenue line show against the +22% June comparison?

rows.finding: The D.C. Circuit was asked by both the DOJ and Google to prioritise the search cross-appeals so argument could be scheduled as early as 2026-12-09, against a payment reported at $20bn in 2022 that is 16.6% of trailing services revenue and about 22% of services gross profit.
rows.mechanism: A near-pure-margin payment capitalised at 30x is $474bn, 9.4% of market value; the remedy on appeal could restore an outright ban, so a legal event inside the twelve-month window carries a discrete, quantifiable EV hit.
rows.benchmark: The 2025-09-02 remedies decision refused a ban and permitted non-exclusive one-year payments; DOJ seeks to vacate that refusal; Apple's own 10-Q warns a reversal could prohibit commercial terms for search distribution.
rows.weakens: The exit section's treatment of the payment as a slow policy risk rather than a dated December 2026 catalyst.
rows.implication: Price a 30% chance of a 50% cut and a 10% chance of loss at about $13 a share, 3.8% of the price; the base case as written assumes the payment renews near current terms with no discount.
rows.confidence: medium - the argument date comes from a paywalled legal report; the payment size is a 2022 court figure Apple has never confirmed
rows.follow_up: Is oral argument held on 2026-12-09, and does the D.C. Circuit rule before the first one-year renewal?

rows.finding: Tariff refunds are not one-off: they were about 2 points of the June 2026 quarter and about 1 point of the September guide, so roughly 1.5 points across the second half of FY2026, worth $0.11 of June-quarter EPS on $2.02.
rows.mechanism: A cash refund from struck-down IEEPA tariffs is recognised as a reduction of products cost of sales, so it raises reported margin without changing price or unit economics and disappears when the refund cycle closes.
rows.benchmark: June-quarter EPS $2.02 including $0.11 of refund; products gross margin 39.9% against 36.9%.
rows.weakens: The characterisation of the refund as a single-quarter item in the earnings-quality discussion.
rows.implication: Normalised FY2026 EPS is closer to $8.70 than $8.87 on a clean margin, and the reported 49.1% nine-month margin overstates the trading margin by about a point.
rows.confidence: high - both figures are in Apple's own release and guidance
rows.follow_up: Does the FY2026 annual report quantify the full-year refund?

rows.finding: Apple repurchased $62.1bn of stock in nine months of FY2026 at a 39.5x trailing multiple, a 2.5% earnings yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, while total shareholder yield is 1.9%.
rows.mechanism: Buying stock above intrinsic value transfers wealth from continuing to selling holders; the EPS benefit (+1.9 points of growth) is real and the value benefit is negative while the multiple exceeds fair value.
rows.benchmark: Ten-year Treasury 4.93%; five-year average P/E 30.2x; $100bn authorisation of April 2026.
rows.weakens: The capital-return pillar of the bull case at today's multiple.
rows.implication: The buyback supports the EPS line and not the value per share, so a de-rating is not cushioned by capital return at this price.
rows.confidence: high on the numbers, medium on the average repurchase price which is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: Does Apple slow the pace of repurchases in FY2027 or re-authorise at $100bn?

plan.decision_question: Given that the company's own September guide implies a lower underlying gross margin than a year earlier and the DRAM market offers no relief before 2028, is FY2027 EPS of $9.79 (and therefore the $296 base value) achievable, or does the starter band belong near $250?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's franchise risk is small and its price risk is large, and the price risk runs through one number: the gross margin, which Apple itself guides down two to three points in the September 2026 quarter while DRAM stays tight through 2027, so the entry band of $275-296 is set 10-15% too high and the bear case is nearer one in three than one in four.
plan.why_different: Prices every risk against the valuation it damages (EV percentage, dollars per share, points of net income) instead of listing it, separates the one thesis-breaking risk from six manageable ones, and dates each signpost.
plan.mechanism: Memory inflation is a cost transfer from Apple to its suppliers: HBM and server DRAM crowd out consumer DRAM, the three DRAM makers earn more per wafer, and Apple pays more per device while its fixed-price services annuity cannot absorb the hit. Each point of gross margin is 3.0% of net income, so a two-point further decline cancels roughly a year of revenue growth and breaks the forward-EPS base of the valuation.
plan.comparison_set: Peer multiples Microsoft 27.3x, Alphabet 14.6x, Meta 21.0x, Samsung 12.5x against Apple 39.5x; Apple's own five-year average 30.2x and ten-year mean 25.35x; the ten-year average intra-year drawdown of 21.4%; the 2025 tariff episode (-30.2% peak to trough) as the closest recent stress.
plan.counter_evidence: Apple has beaten EPS consensus in eight straight reports, passed memory costs through on iPad and Mac prices in 2026, holds net cash of $62.2bn so no financing risk exists, and a 47-48% gross margin is still above any full year before 2025; the bear case could be the consensus already, in which case the risk is being early rather than wrong.
plan.visual: risk-matrix with eight ranked risks plus a danger info card for the gross-margin risk
plan.prohibited: risks are manageable; huge market; well positioned; clear business model; fierce competition; recently; about 5; strong team

rows.finding: FY2027 consensus EPS of $9.79 implies a 12.3% rise from trailing $8.72, yet Apple guided September-quarter gross margin of 47-48% including 1 point of tariff refunds, against 48.1% in June ex-refund; two points of give-back on ~$490bn of revenue is $9.8bn pretax, 6.3% of net income, leaving EPS near $8.87.
rows.mechanism: Gross margin is the swing factor: memory costs above anything in the record and the refund rolling off compress the earnings base while opex, including R&D up 33% to $34.0bn in nine months, keeps growing; one point of margin equals 3.0% of net income, double one point of revenue growth.
rows.benchmark: Jefferies' $263.66 target of 2026-08-10 and the company's own 47-48% guide; consensus $9.79 assumes margin recovery that the guide contradicts.
rows.weakens: Apple has beaten estimates through the squeeze and has raised prices on iPad and Mac; if pass-through holds margin at 48%, $9.79 is achievable and the base returns to $296.
rows.implication: Value the base on $8.87 at 30.2x, about $268, not $296; do not buy above the margin-adjusted base.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the FY2027 margin path because Apple's pricing response is undisclosed
rows.follow_up: What does the December-quarter guide on 2026-11-02 imply for gross margin ex-refund?

rows.finding: At $344.63 (NasdaqGS close, 2026-10-30), Apple trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 21.0x mega-cap peer median and a 30.2x five-year average, with a 2.7% free-cash-flow yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury.
rows.mechanism: A 39.5x multiple on a 2.7% cash yield requires the cash flow to compound; the reverse DCF needs 11.8% free-cash-flow growth for ten years against 1.5% delivered in FY2021-FY2025, so the price is a bet on re-rating persistence rather than on the franchise alone.
rows.benchmark: Ten-year P/E mean 25.35x, five-year average 30.2x, peer median 21.0x, S&P 500 21.76x trailing, ten-year Treasury 4.93%.
rows.weakens: Apple's 36.8x price-to-free-cash-flow is 43% below the peer median of 64.6x because capex is only $10.0bn a year; on cash the stock is the cheapest mega-cap in the set.
rows.implication: The asymmetry is in the entry price: a starter band at $240-265 and a full position at or below $225 offer a margin of safety that today's price does not.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does the multiple hold if the ten-year yield stays near 4.93% and FY2027 EPS is cut?

rows.finding: Services produced 39.1% of gross profit in nine months to 2026-06-27, down from 42.2% in FY2025, because product gross profit grew 26.3% against 15.3% for Services; the reported ~$20bn Google payment is 22% of services gross profit.
rows.mechanism: The annuity is still the highest-margin layer at 76.3%, but it no longer grows faster than the hardware that creates it, and its most concentrated revenue line survives only on non-exclusive, one-year-or-shorter placement terms under appeal.
rows.benchmark: Services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit fell to $0.64 from $0.73; the D.D.C. remedies decision of 2025-09-02 refused a payment ban but barred exclusivity and terms over one year.
rows.weakens: Services revenue still grew 14.1% and Apple Intelligence registration in China on 2026-07-15 opens a market where the assistant was absent for 22 months.
rows.implication: Model the Google payment as an annually repriced asset, not a perpetuity, and cap the position for a single regulatory event worth 9.4% of market value.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What terms does the first one-year renewal carry, and how much US link-out spending has moved off in-app purchase?

rows.finding: Greater China revenue rose 30.0% to $64.8bn in nine months to 2026-06-27 and Apple's unit share rose 4.2 points to 18.1% in Q2 2026, but Huawei holds 22.6% and IDC expects China shipments to fall about 20% in H2 2026.
rows.mechanism: The growth is a launch, price and currency effect on a withdrawn subsidy base; when the comparison laps a +30% base, the region that contributed 4.1 points of group growth becomes the largest source of downside.
rows.benchmark: China units fell 4.3% in Q2 2026, the fifth straight decline, and Huawei grew 19.9% on HarmonyOS and price discipline.
rows.weakens: Nine-month China revenue already exceeds all of FY2025, and the CAC approval of Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 narrows the AI gap in the market where it mattered most.
rows.implication: Stress China at -20% revenue: about $13bn, 3.9% of net income, before touching the multiple.
rows.confidence: high on the revenue figures, medium on the durability of the growth
rows.follow_up: How much of the Greater China increase is currency, and what does the December quarter show against the +30% base?

rows.finding: The closest analog is Microsoft after 2014: a legacy incumbent re-rated roughly eight-fold in a decade as cloud replaced declining licence revenue; the cautionary analog is Nokia, which held 40-50% of handsets in 2007 and under 5% by 2013 as the platform shifted to software it did not control.
rows.mechanism: Platform transitions destroy incumbent value when the new layer sits outside the incumbent's control; they enrich incumbents that own the distribution layer and can attach the new capability to an existing annuity.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft began its transition near 10-12x earnings, so re-rating supplied much of the return; Apple starts at 39.5x, where the same transformation would have to come from earnings alone.
rows.weakens: Apple owns its platform and distribution, unlike Nokia, and rents the frontier model rather than missing the shift, which is closer to Microsoft's early cloud years than to Nokia's collapse.
rows.implication: The franchise probably survives the AI shift; the multiple is the fragile part, so the decision rule is price, not technology.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Does Apple's AI layer produce a measurable upgrade or ARPU lift by FY2028, or remain a licensed cost?

rows.finding: The market regime offers no valuation cushion: the S&P 500 is 3.4% below its 52-week high, the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile, the ten-year Treasury yields 4.93% and technology is 7.4 points behind SPY over one month while energy and health care lead.
rows.mechanism: A high-multiple, long-duration cash-flow stock is sensitive to the discount rate and to rotation; with the risk-free rate near 5%, the 2.7% free-cash-flow yield demands growth that the margin guide puts at risk.
rows.benchmark: Ten-year Treasury 4.93%, 2-year 4.61%, fed funds 4.00%, IG spreads 89bp, HY 326bp.
rows.weakens: The Fed has stopped tightening and credit spreads are tight, so a soft-landing regime could support the multiple longer than the valuation arithmetic implies.
rows.implication: Size the position for a de-rating: zero now, 1-2% at $240-265, 3-4% at or below $225.
rows.confidence: high on the data, medium on regime persistence
rows.follow_up: Does a further rise in the ten-year yield above 5% coincide with FY2027 EPS cuts?

rows.finding: Business quality is exceptional on the disclosed record: more than 2.5bn active devices, a record 23.6% iOS share of 2026 shipments, services at a 76.3% gross margin and return on assets of 36.1% against Microsoft's 35.9% ROIC and Alphabet's 37.0%.
rows.mechanism: The installed base plus the App Store and subscription layer produce a repeat-purchase annuity with negative working capital and minimal capex, which is why the franchise earns a premium multiple.
rows.benchmark: ROA 36.1% vs Microsoft 35.9% ROIC and Alphabet 37.0%; capex 2.2% of revenue vs 34.9% at Microsoft.
rows.weakens: The installed-base figure is company-reported and the app-economy pool is undisclosed, so the annuity's size cannot be independently verified.
rows.implication: Score business quality 9 and financial quality 9; these are the pillars that keep the name on a watchlist rather than in the avoid bucket.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What share of services is commission versus subscription, and what is the measured replacement rate?

rows.finding: Valuation is the weakest dimension: 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward against a 21.0x peer median, a 2.7% free-cash-flow yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, and a reverse DCF that needs 11.8% free-cash-flow growth for a decade against 1.5% delivered.
rows.mechanism: The multiple, not the business, sets the forward return: at 35x forward the stock is fairly valued; at 30.2x it is worth $268; at 25x it is worth $205.
rows.benchmark: Peer median 21.0x, S&P 500 21.76x, five-year average 30.2x, ten-year mean 25.35x, ten-year Treasury 4.93%.
rows.weakens: On price-to-free-cash-flow Apple at 36.8x is 43% below the peer median of 64.6x, so the premium disappears on the metric that funds the buyback.
rows.implication: Score valuation 2; a 20-25% weight on this dimension is what makes the composite a watchlist score rather than a buy.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does the multiple compress toward 30x as FY2027 EPS estimates are cut?

rows.finding: Earnings quality is weaker than the headline: FY2025's 22.7% EPS growth is 10.4% normalising the Irish charge, buybacks added 5.4 points over FY2023-FY2025 but only 1.9 in the trailing twelve months, 2.0 points of the June 2026 gross margin were tariff refunds and inventory rose 87% against 16.2% revenue growth.
rows.mechanism: The reported margin contains one-time refunds and a memory-cost tailwind, and the EPS denominator is shrinking; both flatter the base that the multiple capitalises.
rows.benchmark: Pretax income +7.5% against net income +19.5% in FY2025; free cash flow conversion 1.06x, but 0.88x in FY2025 on $43.4bn cash taxes.
rows.weakens: Cash conversion is strong and the refund is a real cash item, not an accounting invention; the balance sheet is net cash $62.2bn.
rows.implication: Score earnings quality 4 and treat trailing EPS $8.72 as a peak rather than a base.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does the FY2026 10-K decompose the refund and inventory build?

rows.finding: Policy is a recurring cost to the highest-margin layer, not a licence-to-operate threat: the EU DMA fine was €500m on 2025-04-23, the US contempt finding dates from 2025-04-30, the DOJ case is in discovery toward a 2027 trial, and the Google payment survives on non-exclusive one-year terms under appeal.
rows.mechanism: Each remedy transfers pricing power from Apple's toll to developers, consumers or Google, and reaches services gross margin before it reaches revenue.
rows.benchmark: Peer fines are serial but modest: Meta €200m in the same DMA package, Google €890m on 2026-07-23, Alphabet's €4.1bn Android fine final in July 2026.
rows.weakens: China registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, Section 232 spared Apple products on 2026-01-14, and the IEEPA tariffs were struck down on 2026-02-20.
rows.implication: Score policy 6; cap any position at 4% because one regulatory event is worth 9.4% of market value.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What does the D.C. Circuit do after argument from 2026-12-09, and does Article 6(4) produce a second fine?

rows.finding: Management and capital allocation are competent but not cheap: Ternus became CEO on 2026-09-01 with Cook as executive chair, and the company repurchased $62.1bn of stock in nine months at 39.5x, a 2.5% earnings yield against 4.93% on the ten-year.
rows.mechanism: Buybacks at a multiple above intrinsic value transfer value from continuing holders to sellers; the $100bn authorisation of April 2026 extends the practice.
rows.benchmark: Shareholder yield 1.9% against the ten-year Treasury 4.93%; diluted shares down from 16,865M in FY2021 to 14,715M.
rows.weakens: The succession is internal and complete, and net cash rose $28.4bn in nine months, so capital allocation has not damaged the balance sheet.
rows.implication: Score management 6; the buyback supports EPS, not value per share, at this price.

rows.follow_up: Does the first Ternus year bring a new capital-allocation framework or another $100bn authorisation?

scoring.author: Lead Analyst

rows.belief: The need is replacement and ecosystem retention, not unmet demand: buyers delay upgrades and pay for services inside iOS. More than 2.5bn active devices and revenue up 16.2% in nine months of FY2026 while global units fall.
rows.evidence: Installed base above 2.5bn active devices, announced 2026-01-29 [S191]; nine-month FY2026 revenue $364.4bn, +16.2% [S6]; services 25.2% of revenue [S6].
rows.counter_evidence: Global smartphone units fall 16.7% to about 1.0bn in 2026 and the sub-$100 tier nearly collapsed, so part of the willingness to pay is a supply shock, not demand [S66, S39].
rows.confidence: medium
rows.change: Two consecutive quarters of falling services attach or a measured lengthening of the replacement cycle beyond the current estimate.

rows.belief: Apple's integration lead is durable in silicon and distribution (8/10) and thin in AI (4/10): the A20 Pro is on TSMC N2 and the C2 modem reached the flagship, but the next foundation models are licensed from Google.
rows.evidence: A20 Pro on TSMC N2 with a 32-core Neural Engine; C2 in the iPhone 18 line [S64, S59]; Gemini-based Apple Foundation Models announced 2026-01-12 [S58]; services gross margin 76.3% [S6].
rows.counter_evidence: Siri needed a Google licence, Vision Pro shipped about 45,000 units in the December 2025 quarter, and DMA rules may withhold Siri AI in the EU [S6, S87, S86].
rows.confidence: medium
rows.change: A disclosed in-house frontier model, or AI features producing a measurable lift in upgrade rates rather than cost.

rows.belief: 2026 is a supply-shock year that flatters Apple's unit share and price; the honest test of the franchise is 2028, when memory normalises and the premium tier rebuilds.
rows.evidence: DRAM and NAND up more than 300% year on year; 2026 market value $613bn, +6.3%, on units down 16.7% [S66, S39]; IDC sees memory normalising around 2028 [S39].
rows.counter_evidence: Apple's 20.2% unit share gain was bought with early memory supply that lapses, while Samsung both competes in handsets and sells the memory [S102, S66].
rows.confidence: medium
rows.change: Memory prices normalising earlier than 2028, or Apple holding share after they do.

rows.belief: Distribution is the moat: 60% of sales run through carriers and resellers that finance the device, keeping selling expense at 6.6% of revenue, and India assembly is scaling as a tariff hedge.
rows.evidence: 40% direct and 60% indirect in FY2025 [S5]; iPhone output in India about 55m units, 25% of global, projected 28% in 2026 [S91]; selling, general and administrative $27.6bn, 6.6% of revenue [S5].
rows.counter_evidence: India assembly captures little value because components and silicon remain East Asian, and Apple has never disclosed the US-bound share [S91, S6].
rows.confidence: high
rows.change: A channel disruption at a major carrier, or India failing to reach the projected share of output without a quality incident.

rows.belief: A device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at a 39.9% product margin and the services stream is nearly all incremental, but the annuity no longer grows faster than the hardware that creates it and the margin is turning.
rows.evidence: Products 39.9% and Services 76.3% gross margin in nine months of FY2026 [S6]; services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit fell to $0.64 from $0.73 [S5, S6]; September-quarter guide of 47-48% including 1 point of refunds [S199].
rows.counter_evidence: Part of the product margin is a tariff refund (2.0 points of the June quarter) and memory costs are rising [S6].
rows.confidence: high
rows.change: Services gross profit growing faster than product gross profit for two quarters, or the mix ratio recovering above $0.73.

rows.belief: Succession is done and internal, which lowers cultural risk, but the new CEO has never run a P&L and the AI transition sits with a software chief who outsourced the frontier model.
rows.evidence: Ternus CEO from 2026-09-01, Cook executive chair, Levinson lead independent [S152, S174]; AI organisation rebuilt on 2025-12-01 under an external hire reporting to Federighi [S183].
rows.counter_evidence: Five C-suite changes since January 2025, no board member with AI-lab operating experience, and key-person dependence on Srouji and Federighi [S179, S65].
rows.confidence: medium
rows.change: A senior AI or silicon departure, or the first year of Ternus's capital-allocation decisions at the current multiple.

rows.belief: The business is high quality and the price is not: 39.5x trailing and 35.2x consensus forward earnings, 88% above the mega-cap peer median, or 38.9x the margin-adjusted $8.87, with a 2.7% free-cash-flow yield against a 4.93% ten-year Treasury.
rows.evidence: Close $344.63 on 2026-10-30, market cap $5,029.6bn, EV $4,967.4bn [S9, S6]; peer median 21.0x P/E [S124-S126]; ten-year Treasury 4.93% [S9].
rows.counter_evidence: Apple's 36.8x price-to-free-cash-flow is 43% below the peer median of 64.6x because capex is only $10.0bn a year [S9, S6].
rows.confidence: high

spines.must_answer: Is the market mispricing Apple's future cash flow or its risk — does the current price already discount a durable iPhone upgrade cycle, services growth and regulatory defence, leaving no margin of safety for a long-only fund? Answered: the price discounts a 50% gross margin floor and 11.8% free-cash-flow growth for a decade; on a margin-adjusted base of $268 the stock is 22% above fair value, so the fund watchlists it with entry bands at $240-265 and at or below $225.

Is Apple demand durable or promotion-driven — do the installed base, upgrade rate, services attach and pricing power hold through a weak consumer cycle and through Huawei's recovery in China? Answered: demand is replacement-led; units fall 16.7% in 2026 while value rises 6.3%, the installed base exceeds 2.5bn devices, Services grow 14.1% but the mix moved back to hardware, and China grew 30.0% in nine months against a forecast 20% unit decline in H2 2026.

Does policy create a moat or a hidden constraint — how much of services gross profit is exposed to DMA and DOJ remedies and the Google distribution payment, and how much of hardware cost is exposed to China tariffs and a Taiwan contingency? Answered: the reported $20bn search payment is 22% of services gross profit and 9.4% of market value at 30x, preserved only on one-year non-exclusive terms under appeal; DMA and DOJ remedies are a recurring tax on the same layer; tariffs spared Apple products in 2026 but the truce expires on 2027-01-10.

research_plan.industry_map: Consumer technology value chain: semiconductor design (Apple silicon in-house; TSMC the sole advanced-node foundry), memory (SK Hynix, Micron, Samsung), displays (Samsung Display, LG Display, BOE), cameras and RF (Sony, Broadcom, Skyworks, Qorvo), assembly (Foxconn/Hon Hai, Pegatron, Luxshare, Tata in India), distribution (carriers, Apple Retail, e-commerce), platform services (App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay, advertising, Apple TV+, Music, Arcade), developers and regulators. Decisive bottleneck: advanced-node foundry capacity at TSMC (N3/N2) and the geographic concentration of final assembly in China — the first caps performance-per-watt leadership, the second carries tariff and geopolitical risk. In 2026 the binding constraint moved to memory: DRAM and NAND are up more than 300% year on year, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and Samsung is the only top-five handset vendor that also sells memory. Apple sits at the integration point where it captures most industry profit: it designs the SoC and the OS, controls the retail and services interface, and outsources capital-intensive manufacturing.
research_plan.geo_lens: Material. Apple reports five regions — Americas, Greater China, Europe, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific — and its supply chain runs through China, India, Vietnam, Taiwan, Korea and Japan. Mapped: (1) revenue and profit by region, with China demand and Huawei competition separated from the global average; (2) the manufacturing shift from China to India and Vietnam and the tariff exposure that drives it; (3) jurisdiction-specific regulation — EU Digital Markets Act, US DOJ antitrust, China's CAC and app-store rules, India's production-linked incentives; (4) tax jurisdiction (Ireland, OECD Pillar Two) and FX translation. Nine-month FY2026 evidence: Greater China +30.0% to $64.8bn, Europe +16.1% to $95.6bn, Americas +11.4% to $149.4bn; India about 55m iPhone units, 25% of global output, projected 28% in 2026; USD/CNY at 6.6449 on 2026-10-31.
research_plan.policy_lens: Material and decisive for services economics. Mapped and dated: (1) EU Digital Markets Act — €500m fine on 2025-04-23 for anti-steering, Article 6(4) alternative-marketplace file open, General Court upheld gatekeeper designation on 2026-07-08, interoperability rules may withhold Siri AI in the EU; (2) US DOJ antitrust case filed 2024-03-21, dismissal denied 2025-06-30, discovery toward a 2027 trial; (3) Epic v. Apple contempt finding 2025-04-30, Ninth Circuit modification 2025-12-11, Supreme Court certiorari 2026-06-30 limited to the civil-contempt standard; (4) Google search-distribution remedies — D.D.C. decision 2025-09-02 refused a payment ban but permits non-exclusive, one-year-or-shorter placement, final judgment December 2025, appeals by Google (January 2026) and the DOJ and states (February 2026) pending at 2026-10-29, argument sought from 2026-12-09; (5) US tariffs — Section 232 initial results 2026-01-14 imposed no tariff on Apple products, IEEPA tariffs struck down 2026-02-20 with refunds claimed, Section 301 tariffs then imposed, Busan truce extended 2026-09-23 to 2027-01-10; (6) China — CAC registered Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15 with Alibaba Qwen and Baidu, Greater China revenue +30.0% in nine months; (7) OECD Pillar Two and the Irish state-aid case, ECJ 2024-09-10, $15.8bn paid, FY2025 effective tax rate 15.6%.

At $344.63 (2026-10-30) the stock trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x consensus forward earnings against a 21.0x peer median and a 4.93% ten-year Treasury. Apple guided September-quarter gross margin of 47-48% including 1 point of tariff refunds; two points of give-back is 6.3% of net income and leaves FY2027 EPS near $8.87, not the $9.79 consensus, so base value is $268 at 30.2x, with a bear of $205 and a bull of $399. consensus.consensus: The sell side and the market treat Apple as a quality compounder whose services annuity and buyback justify a premium: the average target is $339.35, the stock closed at $344.63 on 2026-10-30, and consensus FY2027 EPS is $9.79, a 12.3% rise on trailing $8.72.
consensus.our_view: Not consensus on the earnings base or the price: Apple guided 47-48% gross margin including a point of refunds, so a two-point give-back leaves FY2027 EPS near $8.87 and the base value at $268, 22% below the close. The franchise is as good as the market says; the price assumes a margin floor that the company has already guided away.
consensus.evidence: Two points on ~$490bn of revenue is $9.8bn pretax, 6.3% of net income [S199, S194, S6]; Jefferies' $263.66 target of 2026-08-10 sits within 2% of that arithmetic [S201]; at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward the stock is 88% above the mega-cap peer median and 1.8x the S&P 500, with a 2.7% free-cash-flow yield against a 4.93% ten-year [S9, S154, S155].
consensus.proof_event: The 2026-11-02 December-quarter guide is the first outlook without the carry-in inventory cushion; it will show whether gross margin ex-refund holds near 47% or falls toward 45%, which decides whether the base is $268 or $205.

one_question.question: Is Apple's ~50% gross margin a new floor, or a tariff-refund and memory-timing peak that flatters trailing EPS?
one_question.why: The entire valuation rests on the earnings base. Trailing EPS of $8.72 and the $9.79 consensus assume the 48.7% trailing gross margin holds; the company's own 47-48% September guide, with one point of refunds, implies 46-47% ex-refund, and a two-point give-back takes EPS to $8.87 and the base to $268, while a further slide to 45% takes it to $205. One point of gross margin is 3.0% of net income, double the effect of one point of revenue growth, so this single number decides whether today's price is 20% too high or fairly valued.

modules.analogs: "Two analogs bound the decision. Microsoft after 2014 is the best case: a legacy incumbent whose cloud transition replaced a declining licence business and whose market value rose from about $381bn to about $3tn in a decade [S198]. The lesson is not that transformation works; it is that Microsoft began near 10-12x earnings, so re-rating supplied much of the return. Apple starts at 39.5x, where the same transformation would have to come from earnings alone. Nokia is the cautionary case: 40-50% of global handsets in 2007, under 5% by 2013, because the platform shift moved value to software it did not control [S200]. Apple owns its platform and rents the frontier model, which places it closer to Microsoft's early cloud years than to Nokia's collapse; the difference is the price of admission."
modules.capital_efficiency: "Capital efficiency is high on assets and poor on incremental equity: capex is 2.2% of revenue and free cash flow converts at 1.06x net income, but $82.2bn of buybacks and $15.6bn of dividends in twelve months equal 1.9% of market value, and each repurchased dollar retires stock at a 2.5% earnings yield against a 4.93% Treasury. The buyback supports EPS more than value per share at this multiple. R&D rose 33% to $34.0bn in nine months with no disclosed AI revenue, so the incremental return on that spend is unproven."
modules.position_sizing: "Listed, long-only. Position size zero at $344.63: the probability-weighted value is about $275 on a margin-adjusted base of $268, so the edge is negative and the Kelly fraction is zero. A starter position of 1-2% of the fund is justified at $240-265, where the base case pays 1-12% and the bear case costs about 20%, and a full position of 3-4% at or below $225, where the downside to the $205 bear is about 9%. Cap at 4% because a single regulatory event, loss of the search payment, is worth about 9.4% of market value. Maximum loss at the full-position entry is the bear value of $205, about 9%, against a bull case of $399. The regime caps the size: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93% and the S&P 500 3.4% below its high, a 39.5x multiple carries de-rating risk."

answers.most_damaging_fact: The load-bearing fact is FY2027 EPS of $9.79, not the $344.63 price: base value of $296 is 30.2x it and the whole entry band derives from it. Apple guided September-quarter gross margin of 47-48% including 1 point of refunds, so 46-47% ex-refund against 48.1% in June, and TrendForce has the DRAM gap widening into 2027 with substantial new output only in 2028 (S194, S192, S106). At FY2027 revenue near $490bn two points of give-back is $9.8bn pretax, 6.3% of trailing net income, leaving EPS near $8.87 and 30.2x that is $268, not $296; Jefferies' $263.66 of 2026-08-10 agrees (S197). If price pass-through instead holds margin, EPS is $10.50 and today's price is fair. One number decides both directions, and the 2026-11-02 December guide is where it is disclosed.
answers.company_only_claims: The installed base of 2.5bn active devices is company-reported: MacRumors restated it on 2026-01-29 (S191), and the thesis table cites S174, which is the 2026-04-20 succession announcement and does not contain the figure; the market section says no device count is published, so the citation is wrong even though the claim is supportable. 'All-time high across all major product categories and geographic segments' (S13) is unverified and unquantified. The 2-point tariff refund is company disclosure whose cash receipt is not shown (S13). The Gemini licence at ~$1bn a year is trade reporting confirmed by neither party (S58, S186). The $20bn Google payment is a 2022 court figure Apple has never confirmed (S82). S165 is a legal-news tracker asserting a payment ban effective June 2026, contradicted by the D.D.C. record (S118); it should be retired from citations.
answers.generic_section: technology_product is the weakest: it concedes the patent moat is unquantified because the registries could not be searched, its depth check fails on granularity (no patent numbers), and its barrier scores of 9/10 for silicon, 8/10 for hardware-OS integration and 10/10 for the installed base are judgements with no base rate, failed-analog test or peer benchmark. The generic artefact is 'a team of 50 senior engineers could match a phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years', which is asserted rather than evidenced. The market section's device-count contradiction (2.3bn unverified against 2.5bn in the thesis table) is the second gap.
answers.unpriced_risk: The margin risk is named in the scenarios but not priced into the recommendation: the base case keeps $9.79 of forward EPS while assuming margin gives back a point, and neither the base value nor the $275-296 band carries the 2-3 point decline Apple has already guided. Second, the Google payment is treated as a slow policy risk when the D.C. Circuit was asked to hear argument from 2026-12-09, putting $474bn, 9.4% of market value, inside the twelve-month window (S196, S82). Third, the buyback's value transfer at 39.5x (a 2.5% earnings yield against 4.93%) is not in the position sizing (S6, S164).
answers.first_challenge: An investment committee partner would challenge the base case's internal inconsistency first: it assumes gross margin gives back 'about a point' while forward EPS rises 12.3% from $8.72 to $9.79 in the same year the company guided a 2-3 point margin decline (S194, S157). Second, why the bear case carries 25% when its main driver is already company-guided rather than hypothetical — 35% is the honest weight and implies value near $266. Third, why the starter band of $275-296 sits above a margin-adjusted base value of $268, so the plan would buy before its own thesis is confirmed. The exit section's revision 5 now carries the corrected 2025-09-02 remedies status, which is right; S165 still says otherwise.
answers.downside_survival: The direction survives every stress; the bands do not. user_data_requests.database: PACER — U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, dockets 2:24-cv-04055 (US et al. v. Apple Inc.) and MDL 2:24-md-03113
user_data_requests.query: The current scheduling order: trial date, fact- and expert-discovery cut-offs, the status of the three special discovery masters appointed in early 2026, and any stipulation defining the scope of equitable relief the DOJ and plaintiff states seek.
user_data_requests.why: The DOJ case is the largest unresolved structural threat to Apple's Services and iPhone economics. The public filings say only that discovery is under way and that the schedule points to a 2027 trial; the docket would date the trial and show how narrow or broad the requested remedy has become, which changes whether the risk belongs in a 2027 or a 2029 cash-flow case.
user_data_requests.how: Pull the docket sheets and the operative case management order from PACER (pacer.uscourts.gov, D.N.J.), or ask counsel with PACER access to export the docket and the scheduling order to PDF.

user_data_requests.database: USPTO Patent Center / EPO Espacenet (patent search and export)
user_data_requests.query: Patent families and grants naming Apple Inc. as assignee, filed 2024-2026, in four areas: on-device/cloud AI and model efficiency; wearable health sensing (blood pressure, glucose, sleep); foldable display and hinge; AR/VR optics and displays. Include application numbers, grant dates, status and forward citations.
user_data_requests.why: Apple discloses no patent count, so the technology section cannot quantify the IP moat or compare grant depth with Samsung, Huawei or Alphabet; without it the patent row stays 'unquantified' and the moat assessment rests on regulatory clearances and silicon know-how only.
user_data_requests.how: Export a CSV from USPTO Patent Center (or Espacenet) filtered by assignee 'Apple Inc.' and filing date 2024-01-01 to 2026-10-31, with CPC classes G06N, A61B5, H04M and G02B.

user_data_requests.query: Apple Operations International Limited, Apple Operations Limited and Apple Distribution International Limited: latest annual accounts, registered office, directors, shareholders and any transfer-pricing or IP-ownership notes.
user_data_requests.why: The 10-K gives no entity-level profit, ownership percentages or roles. These accounts would show which Irish entity books non-U.S. profit and set the durability of the 15.6% effective tax rate, the structure's main policy tail.
user_data_requests.how: Download the most recent annual accounts and company detail sheets for the three Irish entities from core.ie (some documents require a fee account) and upload them.

technology_product.markdown:
Apple's silicon-plus-OS stack is still the widest integrated consumer technology stack, but in 2026 the company rented the one layer it could not build — the frontier model — so what remains defensible is distribution, custom silicon and regulated health sensing, not leadership in artificial intelligence. In two years the A20 Pro moved the iPhone to TSMC N2, the C2 modem reached the flagship, the first foldable shipped at $1,999, and on 2026-01-12 Apple and Google announced the next Apple Foundation Models would be Gemini-based [S58, S59, S63, S64].

### The silicon lead is real, costly, and rented from TSMC

The A19 Pro used TSMC N3P; a year later the A20 Pro moved to TSMC N2 with a 32-core Neural Engine and ~52 TOPS, about double the prior generation's AI throughput. N2 wafers are reported at ~$30,000 against $18,000-20,000 for 3nm, so each step costs more. Product gross margin was 39.9% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 versus 36.9% a year earlier, but only with tariff refunds and mix offsetting "higher costs, including memory", and the 10-Q warns that advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints are expected to intensify [S6, S64].

| Metric | Value | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node, A19 Pro / A20 Pro | TSMC N3P (2025) / N2 (2026) | Teardown and trade reporting | S63, S64 |
| CPU clock, A19 Pro | up to 4.26 GHz, 6 cores | Published specification | S63 |
| Neural Engine, A20 Pro | 32 cores, ~52 TOPS, ~2x A19 Pro | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| N2 wafer price | ~$30,000 vs $18,000-20,000 at 3nm | Trade-press estimate | S64 |
| Product gross margin | 39.9% vs 36.9% (9M FY2025) | Reported financials | S6 |
| On-device model / PCC context | ~3B parameters / 32K tokens | Apple research and developer docs | S61, S62 |

### Apple Intelligence is an architecture with a rented brain

On device, Apple runs a ~3B-parameter model optimised through KV-cache sharing and 2-bit quantisation-aware training; on its servers, a Parallel-Track Mixture-of-Experts model runs inside Private Cloud Compute, which enforces stateless processing, no privileged access even for Apple staff, and attested software images. The binding constraint is memory bandwidth and power: phone-class memory caps on-device inference at single-digit billions of parameters, so harder queries are offloaded. The ceiling is disclosed: a 32K-token context is small against frontier assistants, and Apple's own models were not frontier-quality. The unresolved question for the privacy story is where Gemini-derived inference physically runs. Apple says Apple Intelligence continues on Apple devices and Private Cloud Compute; trade reporting says Google's cloud performs the Gemini computation and puts the licence at ~$1bn a year, on top of a default-search payment of ~$20bn. Neither figure is Apple-confirmed. China's CAC approved Apple Intelligence on 2026-07-15, nearly two years after its 2024 debut, with Alibaba's Qwen and Baidu supplying a separate model stack. Apple's differentiation is orchestration, distribution and privacy, not model quality; an investor should underwrite the cash flow and installed base, not the AI layer [S8, S58, S60, S61, S86, S120, S171].

| Dimension | Apple 2024 (AFM v1) | Apple 2026 (Gemini-based AFM) | Google (supplier) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frontier model | Own ~3B on-device plus server model | Gemini-derived | Owns Gemini | S58, S61 |
| Cost structure | Fixed R&D and data-centre capex | Fixed R&D plus per-query licence | Licence revenue | S58, S86 |
| What Apple keeps | Silicon, OS, orchestration | Silicon, OS, interface, orchestration | Model, training, inference | S58, S60 |

### Products: a strong cycle, a late foldable, a spatial computer that never became a platform

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max launched on 2026-09-09 at $1,199 and $1,299; the foldable iPhone Duo at $1,999 went on sale on 2026-10-23. iPhone net sales rose 22% to $196.5bn in the nine months to 2026-06-27, with Greater China up 30%. The C2 modem supports US mmWave and uses 15% less energy than the C1X, but the larger iPhone 18 Pro Max appears to keep a Qualcomm modem, so Qualcomm retains leverage over the highest-ASP SKU. Vision Pro is the counter-example: ~390,000 units in 2024, ~45,000 in the December 2025 quarter despite the M5 refresh, ~600,000 lifetime, and an IDC forecast of ~290,000 units in 2026 [S59, S13, S87].

| Product | Stage | Launch | Revenue or share | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Commercial | 2026-09 | $196.5bn, 54% of 9M | Products 39.9% | C2 in Pro Max, 2027 | S59, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Commercial | 2026-10-23 | Inside iPhone; undisclosed | Not disclosed | First-quarter volume | S59 |
| Watch Series 11 / Ultra 3 | Commercial | 2025-09 | Wearables $27.3bn, +2% | Not disclosed | Hypertension roll-out | S5, S6 |
| Vision Pro (M5) | Commercial | 2025-10 | ~45k units Q4 2025 | Not disclosed | Lower-cost model, late 2026 | S87 |
| Services | Commercial | — | $91.7bn, +14% | 76.3% | AI tier / iCloud+ gating | S6, S107 |

### What is enforceable is regulatory, not patent

Apple publishes no patent count; the FY2025 10-K says only that it is "pursuing thousands of applications around the world" and that no single right protects its products. Patent counts and peer comparison were not obtainable — the registries could not be searched — so the patent moat is unquantified. What is documented is a regulatory estate — hypertension and sleep-apnoea notifications, a hearing-aid De Novo grant and imaging calibration — each cleared on its own clinical file, a slower but more durable barrier than a patent family.

| Asset | Identifier | Jurisdiction | Date | Status | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Patent portfolio | Count not disclosed | US and foreign | Ongoing | "Thousands of applications" | Unquantified | S5 |
| Hypertension Notification | K250507 | US FDA | 2025-09-11 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S30 |
| Sleep Apnea Notification | K240929 | US FDA | 2024-09-13 | Cleared 510(k) | Watch sensing | S33 |
| Hearing Aid Feature | DEN230081 | US FDA | 2024-09-12 | De Novo granted | AirPods | S34 |
| Medical Imaging Calibration | K253582 | US FDA | 2026-04-01 | Cleared 510(k) | Display calibration | S29 |

### The moat is wide at the bottom of the stack and thin at the top

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Custom SoC and modem | 9 | Top design team plus priority TSMC N2 access; a decade and an Intel acquisition | 4-5 years | S59, S64 |
| Hardware-OS integration | 8 | Six operating systems co-designed with custom silicon | 3-5 years | S5 |
| On-device model efficiency | 5 | Quantisation and KV-cache techniques are published | 1-2 years | S61 |
| Frontier model | 3 | Available to licence, as Apple has shown | 1-2 years, by cheque | S58 |
| FDA-cleared health features | 7 | Each feature needs its own trial and clearance | 3-4 years | S30, S33 |
| Installed base and developers | 10 | A decade of switching costs, record active base | 10+ years | S13, S87 |
| **Composite** | **8/10 hardware, 4/10 AI** | The stack is hard to copy; the intelligence is not | **4-5 years for hardware** | S58, S64 |

The replication test: a team of 50 senior silicon and operating-system engineers could match a phone-class SoC and OS in four to five years, and rent a competitive model next quarter. The counter-evidence is Apple's own record: Siri needed a Google licence, the car was cancelled, and Vision Pro has not reached platform volumes. Regulation can also withhold the assistant: the Q3 FY2026 10-Q states DMA interoperability obligations have in the past, and may in future, cause Apple not to launch or maintain features "such as Siri AI" in certain jurisdictions. The advantage holds only if on-device AI lifts upgrade rates and regulators leave the App Store economics that fund the silicon intact. Two diligence questions settle it: whether the Google agreement allows fine-tuning for on-device use, and whether the 2027 Pro Max moves fully to the C2 [S6, S58, S59, S87].

::: evidence
**Apple's integration advantage is durable in silicon and distribution, but it no longer extends to the model layer.**

The A20 Pro's 2nm node and 32-core Neural Engine keep Apple at the leading edge of phone silicon, and ten FDA clearances and grants since 2020 give it a regulated feature estate rivals must replicate trial by trial. But basing the next Apple Foundation Models on Gemini concedes that the frontier layer is bought, the reported ~$1bn annual licence turns a fixed R&D advantage into a variable cost paid to a competitor, and availability now varies by jurisdiction: China runs a Qwen/Baidu stack and DMA rules may withhold Siri AI in the EU [S6, S58, S64, S86, S120, S171].
:::

business_model.markdown:
Apple runs a hardware annuity with a services margin layered on top — 73 cents of services gross profit for every dollar of product gross profit — but the mix shift the multiple pays for stalled in fiscal 2026, when hardware margins, helped by tariff refunds, grew gross profit faster than Services. Apple sells through two routes, and the split is the least-discussed fact in the model: in fiscal 2025, 40% of net sales went through its own stores, online store and direct sales force and 60% through carriers, resellers and distributors. The carrier finances or subsidises the handset to win a contract, so the carrier bears the acquisition cost and Apple's selling expense stays at $27,601M, or 6.6% of revenue. There is little contracted backlog: deferred revenue was $13.7bn at 2025-09-27, 3.3% of revenue, two thirds of it recognised within a year. Apple is a repeat-purchase business recognised as it bills, not a subscription business with a book of contracted revenue [S5].

### The mix shift, and its reversal

The arithmetic of the mix shift is the strongest part of the case. In fiscal 2025 Services produced $109,158M of revenue at a 75.4% gross margin against $307,003M of Products at 36.8%: 26.2% of revenue but 42.2% of gross profit ($82,314M of $195,201M), up from 35.7% two years earlier, with services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit rising from $0.55 in fiscal 2023 to $0.73. Then the mechanism ran backwards. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 product gross profit rose 26.3% to $108,819M while services gross profit rose 15.3% to $69,963M, and Services fell to 39.1% of gross profit; product gross margin reached 39.9% against 36.9% a year earlier, taking total gross margin to 49.1% and to 50.1% in the June quarter against 46.5%. Apple attributes the gain to "a different mix of products and tariff refunds, partially offset by higher costs, including memory", the most consequential disclosure in this section: it makes fiscal 2026's margin hardware-led and partly a refund rather than a trading gain [S5, S6].

### Unit economics per revenue dollar, because there are no units

Apple discloses no unit volumes, average selling price or installed-base figure, so a per-device waterfall cannot be built from primary evidence. The economics of each revenue dollar can be.

| Unit-economics line | FY2025 | 9M FY2026 | Evidence and status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Product cost of sales, per $1,000 of product revenue | $632 | $601 | Bill of materials, assembly and warranty provision combined, not split | S5, S6 |
| Product gross profit | $368 | $399 | 36.8% to 39.9%; includes tariff refunds in fiscal 2026 | S5, S6 |
| Services cost of sales, per $1,000 of services revenue | $246 | $237 | Content, hosting and payment processing | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit | $754 | $763 | 75.4% to 76.3% | S5, S6 |
| Services gross profit per $1 of product gross profit | $0.73 | $0.64 | Closest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost | S5, S6 |
| Customer acquisition cost, support and warranty | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Carriers bear acquisition; warranty sits inside cost of sales | S5 |
| LTV, LTV:CAC, CAC payback in months | Not computable | Not computable | Requires units, ASP and installed base, none of which Apple reports | S5 |

Apple therefore has no payback period to wait out: a device is gross-profit-positive on delivery at a 36.8% product margin, and the services stream that follows is nearly all incremental, since services cost of sales is $26,844M on $109,158M of revenue. The nearest disclosed proxy for lifetime value against acquisition cost is the $0.73 of services gross profit per dollar of product gross profit, and its fall to $0.64 is the number to watch — the annuity still grows, but no longer faster than the hardware that creates it [S5, S6].

### Pricing power shows up as mix, not as price

| Line | FY2025 net sales | Year on year | What the filing discloses about price and mix | Gross margin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | $209,586M | +4% | Growth "due to higher net sales of Pro models", i.e. mix rather than units | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| Services | $109,158M | +14% | "advertising, the App Store and cloud services" | 75.4% | S5 |
| Mac | $33,708M | +12% | "laptops and desktops" | 36.8% products blended | S5 |
| iPad and Wearables | $63,709M | 0% | iPad Air and mini higher, Accessories and Wearables lower | 36.8% products blended | S5 |

Pricing power shows up as mix: iPhone revenue rose 22% to $196,515M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, attributed again to higher sales of Pro models rather than to units. The same disclosure prevents separating price from volume, and therefore prevents estimating elasticity — a 22% increase could be volume, price, or any combination. Apple publishes list prices on its own store but not in its filings, and this report did not retrieve a verified 2026 price list, so the table uses disclosed mix effects rather than price points; third-party unit data would settle it [S6].

### The highest-margin layer is also the most litigated

App Store economics are recognised net — Apple books "only the commission it retains" on third-party app sales — so a take-rate cut passes straight to revenue and gross profit with no offsetting cost. Apple is subject to a US court order barring it from charging a commission on certain consumer purchases, though the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to permit one, and in the EU the Digital Markets Act forces alternative distribution, alternative payment processing and new fee structures, a plan the European Commission has challenged. A second concentration sits in the same line: Apple earns licensing revenue from Google for search distribution inside Services advertising, which Apple names as a primary driver of Services growth in both fiscal 2025 and the first nine months of fiscal 2026. The payment was $20bn in 2022 per unsealed court documents, 18.3% of fiscal 2025 Services revenue, and Apple does not disclose the current figure; the District of Columbia court order of 2025-09-02 preserved the ability to pay partners while banning exclusive agreements, but Apple states a reversal on appeal could impose remedies "prohibiting Google from offering the Company commercial terms for search distribution", and both the Department of Justice and Google appealed [S6, S82].

### Cost structure, and what would break the durability

The cost base is bought, not built: product cost of sales of $194,116M goes to TSMC for wafers, to memory suppliers for DRAM and NAND, and to Foxconn and its peers for assembly. Research and development reached $34,035M in the nine months to 2026-06-27, up 33% and 9.3% of revenue against 8.3% in fiscal 2025, on "infrastructure-related costs, including investments in artificial intelligence"; capital expenditure is 2.2% of trailing-twelve-month revenue against 34.9% at Microsoft in fiscal 2026. Apple rents its manufacturing and buys much of its AI capability through the income statement, so that bill reaches the operating margin immediately rather than through depreciation. For investors the implication is that the annuity is intact, but the margin expansion of the last four quarters is not the mix shift it is commonly described as: it is product mix, a tariff refund and memory cost timing, on top of a services base whose most profitable components face an appeal, a court order and a European regulatory process. The downside is quantifiable rather than hypothetical: giving back three points of gross margin and losing the search licence together would take more than a fifth of trailing-twelve-month net income. Three facts would settle the durability question and none is disclosed — the current size of the search payment, the share of Services that is App Store commission, and the refund-versus-mix split; the fiscal 2026 annual report, not on EDGAR as of 2026-10-31, may settle them [S6, S27].

::: evidence
**The service mix still drives Apple's margin, but in fiscal 2026 it stopped being the marginal driver — hardware did, and part of that gain is a refund.**

In the nine months to June 2026 product gross profit grew faster than services gross profit for the first time in three years, and Apple attributes the higher product margin to product mix and tariff refunds rather than to trading gains, in the June 2026 quarterly report.
:::

depth: 5 vague phrasings such as "about $4"; give the exact figure or name

market.author: Market Analyst
market.markdown:
Apple's markets are contracting in units and expanding in value, and Apple is taking value share inside that contraction: the case for FY2026-FY2028 rests on premiumisation and installed-base monetisation rather than unit volume or a Services mix shift, is strongest in the United States, is adequate in Europe, and in China depends on a domestic champion's pricing discipline.

### The pool is shrinking in units and growing in value

IDC's August 2026 forecast has worldwide smartphone shipments at just over 1.0 billion units in 2026, down 16.7%, while total market value rises 6.3% to $613 billion and the average selling price reaches a record $581, up 27.6% in a year. The cause is cost, not demand: DRAM and NAND prices are up more than 300% year on year as capacity is redirected to AI servers, memory is more than 65% of bill of materials at the low end, and the sub-$100 tier fell close to 60% in the second quarter of 2026. This is a supply shock with a dated end, so 2026-2027 flatters Apple's unit share while genuinely lifting its price, and 2028 is the test of whether either survives. [S66]

Two sizing methods agree closely: 1.0 billion units at the $581 average price gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's $613 billion, so the two series are consistent rather than rival estimates. On that base Apple's serviceable market is the premium tier it addresses — an iOS share of 23.6% of 2026 shipments, a record — while the revenue it can obtain is what it already books: $466.8 billion trailing twelve months to 2026-06-27, which at the 16.2% growth rate of the first nine months of FY2026 implies $483 billion for FY2026. [S6]

| Measure | Method | Figure | Year | Publisher | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM, smartphone value (top-down) | Industry value estimate | $613bn, +6.3% | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| TAM, smartphone value (bottom-up) | 1.0bn units x $581 ASP | ~$581bn | 2026 | Calculation on IDC inputs | S66 |
| TAM, personal computing devices | Units only | ~398m units, -11.3%; 1.5% CAGR to 2030 | 2026 | IDC | S103 |
| SAM, premium smartphone tier | iOS share of shipments | 23.6% of units, record | 2026 | IDC | S66 |
| SOM, Apple revenue | Reported | $466.8bn TTM | TTM to 2026-06-27 | Apple 10-Q | S6 |
| Near-term obtainable revenue | FY2025 $416.2bn grown at the 9M FY2026 rate | ~$483bn | FY2026E | Calculation on Apple filings | S5, S13 |

### China is the swing factor, and India sits in the wrong line

Apple's revenue is moving toward the faster-growing regions, but the swing is China. In the first nine months of FY2026 Greater China produced $64.8 billion, up 30.0% on a base of $49.9 billion, after falling from $72.6 billion in FY2023 to $64.4 billion in FY2025; the Americas grew 11.4% to $149.4 billion, Europe 16.1% to $95.6 billion, Japan 10.4% and Rest of Asia Pacific 19.4%. Greater China's $14.9 billion increase contributes 4.1 percentage points of the group's 16.2% growth, more than any other segment, and part of it is currency: a favourable renminbi effect in Greater China, an unfavourable yen effect in Japan. Europe includes India, the Middle East and Africa, so the fastest-growing large smartphone market is invisible in the segment line. [S13]

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Apple's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| United States / North America | 60% of Q1 2026 shipments above $800; 24.9% of global PC-plus-tablet units | Smartphone -6.3% in 2026; PC -14.6% in 2026 | Entered, leads the premium tier; 41.0% of Apple revenue is the Americas | Tariffs, carrier financing, antitrust suits | Samsung, Lenovo, HP, Dell | S39, S103, S13 |
| Greater China | ~66m units a quarter, 264m a year | -4.3% in Q2 2026, fifth straight decline; H2 2026 could be -20% | 18.1% of units, second behind Huawei; revenue +30.0% | Domestic operating system, subsidy withdrawal, data rules | Huawei 22.6%, OPPO 16.0%, vivo 16.0%, Xiaomi 12.4% | S40, S6 |
| Europe (includes India, Middle East, Africa) | India 31.0m units in Q1 2026 at a record $302 ASP | India units -4.1% but value +5.8%; Europe revenue +16.1% | Entered; fourth by units in India | DMA, price sensitivity, distribution | Samsung, Xiaomi, vivo, Lenovo, HP | S105, S103, S13 |
| Japan | Revenue $24.4bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +10.4%; units -25.6% in 2026 | Entered, premium strong; weak yen cuts revenue | Yen, saturated device base | Local Android vendors, Samsung | S13, S103, S6 |
| Rest of Asia Pacific | Revenue $30.2bn in 9M FY2026 | Revenue +19.4%; units -14% in 2026 | Entered, premium-led | Price-sensitive mass market, currency | Samsung, Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo | S13, S39, S103 |

### Services carries the profit, but the mix moved back to hardware

The fastest-growing pool Apple monetises is Services, but its share of revenue fell in FY2026: $91.7 billion in the first nine months, 25.2% of $364.4 billion and up 14%, at a 76.3% gross margin against 75.4% for FY2025, when Services was $109.2 billion, 26.2% of revenue. Hardware grew faster than Services, so the mix shifted toward premium handsets and China rather than toward the recurring pool — the opposite of what a Services-led thesis needs. The app economy itself has no published size in the sources retrieved: neither Apple nor the platform owners disclose app-store gross billings or mobile-advertising revenue, so Apple's Services line is the measured pool. The installed base is disclosed: Apple put it at more than 2.5 billion active devices on 2026-01-29, up from 2.35 billion a year earlier, which is the stock behind Services and the upgrade pool, but Apple still does not publish a replacement rate, so upgrade timing cannot be sized from public data. [S5, S6, S174, S191]

### Who pays, and how much demand is policy

The budget owner is the consumer, in a discretionary purchase that is increasingly financed. In the United States and United Kingdom interest-free financing is common, so IDC expects the premium end to hold while emerging markets fall more than 20%; in India brands lean on financing after the sub-$100 tier fell 59% and the $600-800 band grew 32%; in China the government subsidy that supported earlier quarters faded in the second quarter of 2026, so demand there is being withdrawn by policy rather than created by it. Policy moves Apple's margin more than a product cycle does: after the February 20, 2026 Supreme Court ruling struck down certain IEEPA tariffs, Apple recognised refunds as a reduction of product cost of sales, and those refunds contributed 2.0 percentage points of the June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin. [S105, S40, S13]

### What would break the premiumisation case

Counter-evidence is fourfold. If memory prices normalise in 2028 as IDC expects, the entry tier rebuilds and Apple's 2026 share gain is contestable again. If China's June-quarter demand was pulled forward ahead of second-half price increases, as IDC's China team reports, the 30% growth line is a launch and currency effect. If courts and the European Commission remove the App Store take rate, the margin layer that offsets hardware cyclicality stops compounding. And the search-distribution payment — $20 billion in 2022, equal to 17% of trailing Services revenue of $120.5 billion and 22% of trailing Services gross profit of $91.6 billion — has not been banned: the September 2, 2025 remedies decision declined to ban distributor payments, and the December 2025 final judgment that restricts distribution is under appeal by Google and the Department of Justice, both pending at 2026-10-29. The investor implication is narrow: in a 1-billion-unit market Apple can grow device revenue only if price rises faster than units fall, making average selling price, China durability and the Services take rate the variables worth monitoring. Sizing confidence is high, because two independent methods agree within 5%; confidence that the mix shift holds to 2028 is medium, because it rests on China and a legally contested commission. Three diligence questions remain open: what share of Services revenue is commission-based rather than subscription, advertising or licensing? How much of the Greater China increase is currency? And what is the current average replacement cycle, measured rather than asserted? [S66, S40, S82, S118, S42, S5]

::: evidence
**Apple's addressable device market fell 16.7% in units in 2026 while growing 6.3% in value, and Apple's revenue grew 16.2% over nine months — the gap is premiumisation and China, not market growth, and Services is not gaining mix (S66, S13, S6).**

IDC forecasts 2026 shipments at just over 1.0 billion units against a market value of $613 billion and an ASP of $581 (S66, S39). Apple's nine-month FY2026 revenue was $364.4 billion, up 16.2%, with Greater China up 30.0% on a $49.9 billion base and Services at 25.2% of revenue against 26.2% in FY2025 (S13, S6). The bottom-up check of 1.0 billion units at $581 gives $581 billion, within 5% of IDC's value estimate (S66).
:::
